lecture.Merhaba! Bugün çok işine yarayacak bir b: Hello! Today a very useful skill: describing a thing whose name you do not know. 'You know that thing you open it with…' In German this is a relative clause. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün insanların neden şehre ta: Hello! Today we will talk about why people move into the city. You will use the conjunction of proportion for the second time in this module — this time for a social trend. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Bugünün konusu zor: karşındaki: Hello! Today's subject is a hard one: the other person is angry. In German the order for taking the tension down is settled — name the feeling first, then come back to the matter, and offer the solution last. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Geçen ders 'damit' idi. Bugün o: Hello! Last lesson it was 'damit'. Today its sibling: 'um … zu'. It says the same thing — purpose — but shorter, because when the subject is the same no subclause is needed. Ready?
lecture.Şimdi işin kolay tarafı. Belirli artikel: Now the easy side of it. If there is a definite article the adjective takes almost always one of two endings: the short one in the nominative, the long one in the other cases. So the choice comes down to two.
lecture.Türkçede 'öğrenmek için' dersin ve iş bi: In English you say 'in order to learn' and that is that. German needs two pieces: a conjunction at the front and the infinitive at the end. Everything else is caught in between. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Krizde cümleler kısalır ve işlev fiili ö: In a crisis sentences get shorter and function-verb phrases come forward: measures are taken, damage is limited, the plan is put into effect. Fixed phrases give you speed here. The words first.
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün ağır bir konu ve bu tam d: Hello! Today a heavy subject, and this is exactly where the subjective modals pay off: showing with the language itself how sure you are on a contested question. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün bir şeyi NEDEN yaptığını: Hello! Today we will learn to say WHY you do something: 'so that my children can study', 'so that they stay healthy'. German has 'damit' for this. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün konuşmayan bir dili konuş: Hello! Today we will speak a language that does not speak: body language. And to describe it we need the conjunction of method again — 'we show openness by not folding our arms'. Ready?
lecture.Almancanın iki hazır cümlesi var: biri g: German has two ready sentences: one owns the gaffe, the other closes the subject. The trap in between is trying to save yourself — that always goes badly. The words first.
lecture.Bu modülü bitirdin: artık neyin ağrıdığı: You have finished this module: you can say what hurts, make an appointment, take your medicine properly and call for help when you have to. Now you are sitting down in that chair.
lecture.Bugün iki geçmiş olayı sıralamayı öğrene: Today we will learn to put two past events in order. In English you say 'after I had eaten' and use a separate past form for the earlier event; German does exactly the same. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün empatiyi kuracağız ve dil: Hello! Today we will build empathy, and the grammar suits it exactly: putting yourself in somebody else's place means building a situation that is not real — that is, the subjunctive. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün herkesin tanıdığı bir düş: Hello! Today an enemy everybody knows: putting things off. German even has a name for it, and the sentences built with that name are said with structures that stand in for the passive. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün sayıları anlatacağız. Sun: Hello! Today we will present figures. In a presentation what matters is not who did it but what happened, so the language is passive — but this time in its completed past form. Ready?
lecture.Telefonda üç şey söylenir: ne olduğu, ne: Three things are said on the phone: what has happened, how urgent it is and what should be done. The third is asked as a question and there the modal moves to the front. First, eight words.
lecture.Üç hamle: soruyu kendi cümlenle tekrarla: Three moves: repeating the question in your own words, putting the answer in order and, if you must, clarifying what you yourself said. The indirect question pattern helps with all three. The words first.
lecture.Yeni bir kural yok; iyelik kelimesi ile: There is no new rule; the possessive word and the object ending will work side by side. If you can build both correctly in one sentence you have finished this module. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.'Filmde gösterilen görüntüler' derken Al: For 'the pictures shown in the film' German may build no relative clause at all; it puts the participle straight in front of the noun and gives it an adjective ending. This is the signature of the written language. The words first.
lecture.Bu düzeni bilmek iş görüşmesinde de sözl: Knowing this system is needed both in a job interview and when you read a contract. Most of the words are compounds, so once you know the parts the meaning comes by itself. Let us learn them first.
lecture.Geçen derslerde severek yapmayı anlatan: In earlier lessons you learnt the word for doing something gladly. Today it has a companion: the form used when you choose between two things. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün toplantıyı sen yöneteceks: Hello! Today you will chair the meeting. Chairing is not commanding: the sentences that steer are built in the subjunctive, because they still leave the others room to object. Ready?
lecture.Müzik, tanıştığın herkesle konuşabileceğ: Music is a subject you can talk about with everybody you meet. Today we will learn to say what you listen to, which you prefer and, if you play something, to tell about that. Ready?
lecture.Türkçe adlar Alman kulağına yabancı geld: English names sound foreign to a German ear too, so spelling out is an everyday job. And we will learn a small question form that has no direct counterpart in English. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Almancada fiiller kişiye göre sonlarını: In German verbs change their endings with the person. English changes almost nothing — only the third person takes an -s — so this wants practice. Today we will work on it at the stove. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Bugün evin odalarını öğreneceğiz. Her od: Today we will learn the rooms of a home. Every room has its own article, and since English has nothing of the kind you have to learn the word together with its article. Ready?
lecture.Bugün okul yıllarını anlatıyoruz: neye i: Today we are telling of your school years: what was allowed, what was forbidden, what was compulsory. We will do the past of the modals once more, but this time with permission and prohibition. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün ilgi cümlesinin en işlek: Hello! Today the busiest form of the relative clause: the one with a preposition in it. 'The city I live in', 'the colleague I work with', 'the subject we talked about'. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün tıptaki bir gelişmeyi akt: Hello! Today we will report an advance in medicine. In news like this every sentence is in the past passive, because what matters is not who did it but what has been done. Ready?
lecture.Acil numarası Almanya'da ve bütün Avrupa: The emergency number is the same in Germany and across Europe: one one two. You do not have to build long sentences on the phone; the polite imperative and three short pieces of information are enough. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Kibar rica için dilek kipini zaten kulla: You have already used the subjunctive for a polite request. Now the same form does another job: building a condition that is not real. Two verbs are enough, to be and to have. The words first.
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün ilgi cümlelerini gerçek b: Hello! Today we will use relative clauses on a real job: you have lost something and you have to describe it. The clerk asks one question: which one, what does it look like. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Modülün son dersi ve konusu gel: Hello! The module's last lesson and its subject is the future. When German talks about the future it shows with the verb how sure it is — certain, likely, or merely heard. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Türkçede 'çocukken' tek kelime;: Hello! In English 'when I was a child' uses one conjunction; German has two and the choice depends on the time: als if it happened ONCE in the past, wenn if it was repeated or lies ahead. Ready?
lecture.Almanya'da şehir içinde en hızlı yol çoğ: In Germany the quickest way across a city is usually the bicycle. Today we will learn to say you came by bike, to hire a bike and to understand the warnings on the road. Ready?
lecture.Beş renk ve iki kalıp cebinde: rengi söy: Five colours and two patterns in your pocket: you can say the colour and ask for another. Now you are in a little boutique: you like the shirt in the window but the colour is not quite what you wanted.
lecture.Bugün eşyaların nerede olduğunu söylemey: Today we will learn to say where things are. There is a fine detail here where German parts from English: the verb changes with how a thing is standing. Ready?
lecture.İkisi aynı anlamı taşır, dizilişleri far: The two carry the same meaning but their order differs: obwohl builds a subclause and sends the verb to the end; trotzdem stands at the head of the main clause and pulls the verb right behind it. The words first.
lecture.İlk grup vücutla kurulanlar. Türkçede de: The first group is built on the body. English has idioms like these too but the equivalents are not one to one: German squeezes the thumb for luck where English crosses its fingers. The words first.
lecture.Karşılaştırmada bir tuzak var ve neredey: There is a trap in the comparison and almost everybody falls into it: the word used when you compare two things is not the word for likeness. We will see it at the end. The words first.
lecture.Yani 'Uzak mı?' Türkçede soruyu sona ekl: That is, 'Is it far?' English moves the verb to the front for this too, and German does the same. If the verb is first, the sentence is a question.
lecture.Alışverişte en çok söylenen cümlelerden: One of the sentences said most while shopping is 'I like this'. Today we will learn to say it, to choose between two things and to ask a friend's opinion. Ready?
lecture.İki bağlaç kullanacağız: biri önceyi, bi: We will use two conjunctions: one points at what came before, one at the same moment. In both the verb goes to the end of the clause, and if the clause is first the main clause starts with the verb. The words first.
lecture.Türkçede 'yüzme biliyorum' deriz, yani a: English uses a modal for this too: 'I can swim'. In German a modal comes into the sentence in the same way and the main verb drops to the very end. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Ve çözüm asla emir kipiyle sunulmaz. 'Si: And the solution is never offered in the imperative. Not 'we are giving you a replacement' but 'would it help if we gave you a replacement'. A question gives the other person control back. The words first.
lecture.Yani 'Havalimanına, lütfen'. Türkçede yö: That is, 'To the airport, please'. English puts a word of direction in front of the noun too — to the airport — and in German that word, if the noun is masculine or neuter
lecture.Almanya'da bu soru tanışmanın ilk on dak: In Germany this question comes in the first ten minutes of meeting somebody; there are dogs everywhere. We will use the object rule you learnt with brothers and sisters here as well. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Bir mağazada en çok duyacağın soru beden: The question you will hear most in a shop is about the size. Today we will learn to ask the size, to ask permission to try something on and to say whether it fits. Ready?
lecture.Güzel haber: yeni bir kural öğrenmiyorsu: Good news: you are not learning a new rule. You add a letter to the front of the little word you learnt last time, that is all; the ending changes in the same way. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün Almanya'da altın değerind: Hello! Today a skill worth gold in Germany: putting an appointment back politely. The difference between a blunt 'that does not work' and a courteous wish lies in a single form of the verb. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Son ders. B2'nin ilk modülünde: Hello! The last lesson. In B2's first module you learnt the past passive; we are closing the level with it — because at this level what happened did not happen to you, you did it. Ready?
lecture.Şimdi kural. Edilgen cümlede yardımcı fi: Now the rule. In a passive sentence the auxiliary settles into second place and the past form of the main verb goes to the end — the structure looks like the past tense but the auxiliary is different.
lecture.Alan kişi yönelme hâlinde ve alınan şeyd: The person receiving is in the dative and comes before the thing received. And we will learn a pattern for asking what is local to a region; the preposition in it brings the accusative. First, eight words.
lecture.Bu derste küçük ama çok kullanışlı bir k: There is a small but very useful word in this lesson: a subject that means everybody at once. English says such a subject too — 'you' or 'one' — and German has a word of its own for it. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Bugün daire gezerken sorulacak soruları: Today we will learn the questions to ask when you view a flat. Many people apply for one flat in Germany; whoever asks the right questions both gets the information and looks serious. Ready?
lecture.Kural şu: belirli artikelden sonra sıfat: The rule: after a definite article the adjective is declined weakly, after an indefinite one the adjective carries the gender itself. English adjectives never change, so this wants care. The words first.
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün planlarını anlatmayı öğre: Hello! Today we will learn to describe your plans: what I intend to do, what I want to try. German does this with a little word and the place of that word matters a great deal. Ready?
lecture.Şimdi kural. Zorunluluk fiili ikinci sır: Now the rule. The verb of obligation settles into second place, and the past form of the main verb and the passive auxiliary go together to the end of the sentence. So two words stand side by side at the end.
lecture.Türkçede böyle bir şey yok, o yüzden ilk: English has something close in its phrasal verbs — 'get up', 'ring up' — but in German the piece travels right to the end of the sentence. And these verbs are in the middle of daily life: getting up, doing the shopping, making a phone call. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Almanya'da yol sorarken cümlenin başına: When you ask the way in Germany a word of apology goes at the front of the sentence; without it the question sounds rude. The directions come in three words too: straight on, left, right. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün bir avukatın söylediğini: Hello! Today you will relay to somebody else what a lawyer told you. Here the reported mood is not a matter of style but a limit of responsibility: you cannot present their view as your own verdict. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün komşuyla anlaşmazlık var: Hello! Today there is a disagreement with a neighbour, and Germany has a rule for it: you talk to them directly before you go to the management or the council. That attempt shows in the language too. Ready?
Hello! Today we will deal with institutions. Formal German takes people out of the sentence and turns the actions into nouns: not 'after you have applied' but 'after receipt of the document'. Ready?
lecture.Türkçede her şey 'duruyor'. Almancada is: English has these three as well — stand, lie and hang — and German uses them in exactly the same places. It sounds hard but it settles once you have the three words. First, let us learn the objects.
lecture.Kilit fark şu: 'sözleşmeyi feshediyorum': The key difference is this: 'I am terminating the contract' is a threat, 'I see myself obliged to terminate' is a record. The second is a harder document and yet it looks more courteous. The words first.
lecture.Merhaba ve C1'e hoş geldin. Bu seviyede: Hello and welcome to C1. At this level there are few new rules; the real question is CHOICE — how many different registers you can say the same thing in. The first module: the grammar of institutional German. Ready?
lecture.Resmî dairede sorular soru kelimesiyle b: At an office questions start with a question word and the verb stands in second place. Registering is said with a reflexive verb; the pronoun comes right after the modal. First, eight words.
lecture.Sayılar dilin en çok işe yarayan parçası: Numbers are the most useful part of a language: prices, times, addresses, phone numbers, ages. There is only one thing in German numbers that will surprise you, and we will come to it shortly. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Üç tür bağlaç var: yan cümle bağlaçları: There are three kinds of connector: subclause conjunctions send the verb to the end (weil), main-clause conjunctions leave the order alone (denn), adverbs take first place (deshalb). Today, the adverbs. The words first.
lecture.Baştaki kelime kimseyi göstermez, 'herke: The word at the front points at nobody, it means 'everybody'. In English a rule is often said in the passive — 'that is not done' — and the doer is not named. In German the sentence must have a subject, and this word is that subject.
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün özgeçmişini anlatmayı öğr: Hello! Today we will learn to tell your working life. There is something new here: German has two forms of the past and which one you use depends on where you are speaking. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Yeni modül: müzakere. Pazarlıkt: Hello! A new module: negotiation. In bargaining the German rule is simple — build a categorical sentence and the other side has no room to step back. That is why an offer is made in the subjunctive. Ready?
lecture.Şimdi kural. Bağlaç cümlenin başına geli: Now the rule. The conjunction comes at the front of the sentence and the verb of that part drops to the end. After the comma the main clause comes and there the verb is right at the front, because the first part counts as the first element.
lecture.Kurum dilinin en belirgin alışkanlığı fi: The most striking habit of institutional language is turning verbs into nouns. In English we say 'after checking'; German institutional language says 'after the check'. It gets shorter and more formal. The words first.
lecture.Türkçede soru cümlenin sonunda biter: 'N: English puts the question word right at the front too — 'Where are you from?' — and the verb comes straight after it. That order never changes in German. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Bu modülde geçmişi anlatmanın bütün araç: In this module you have gathered all the tools for telling the past: the Perfekt, the short past of the modals and reflexive verbs. Today we will use all three together in one story. First, eight words.
lecture.Buradaki fiil hem kuralsız hem de vurgus: The verb here is both irregular and begins with an unstressed prefix: there is no participle syllable and the ending of the verb does not change either. The present and the participle look the same and the auxiliary makes the difference.
lecture.Kural şaşırtıcı derecede basit: edat en: The rule is surprisingly simple: the preposition goes right to the front, the pronoun straight after it, and the preposition settles the case. A preposition of place brings the dative; one of movement or of subject matter brings the accusative. The words first.
lecture.Kural şu: yardımcı fiil ikinci sıraya ot: The rule: the auxiliary settles into second place and the past form of the main verb goes right to the end of the sentence. So you have to build the beginning and the end of the sentence together. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Merhaba! Perfekt'in kuralını biliyorsun: Hello! You know the rule of the Perfekt, but some verbs do not follow it. Today we will take the eight used most often; without them you cannot talk about the past. Ready?
lecture.Övgü ve görüş bir yan cümleyle söylenir;: Praise and opinion are said in a subclause, and in that clause the verb goes right to the end. English has subclauses too but the verb does not go last in them — so here both the conjunction and the order want care. The words first.
lecture.Şimdi kural. Amaç bölümü virgülle başlar: Now the rule. The purpose part begins after the comma, the conjunction comes right at the front and the infinitive at the end. If you use a verb that splits in two, the infinitive marker goes into the middle of it — as in the past tense.
lecture.Şimdi kural. Bu fiillerde yardımcı fiil: Now the rule. With these verbs the auxiliary changes: the verb 'to be' is used instead of 'to have'. The structure of the sentence stays the same — the auxiliary in second place, the past form at the very end.
lecture.Yani 'Boş zamanımda kitap biriktiriyorum: That is, 'In my free time I collect books'. Because you started the sentence with a time phrase the verb moved straight behind it and you fell in after the verb. In German the verb always stands in second place.
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün bir konunun iki tarafını: Hello! Today we will learn to give both sides of a subject. This is the strongest move in a debate: you state the other side's argument yourself and then put your own conclusion. Ready?
lecture.Bu dersin bütün cümleleri soru. Almancad: Every sentence in this lesson is a question. German builds questions in two ways and you will see both today: those that start with a question word and those that start with the verb itself. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Kritik kural şu: ara açıklama, açıkladığ: The critical rule is this: an inserted explanation is in the SAME CASE as the word it explains. Explaining the subject it is nominative, explaining the object it is accusative. This is C1's most often missed detail. The words first.
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün iki geçmiş olayı sıraya k: Hello! Today we will learn to put two past events in order: 'After I had eaten I went out.' In German 'nachdem' takes the earlier one and that verb goes one layer further back. Ready?
lecture.Eczanede üç şey sorulur: reçete gerekiyo: Three things are asked at the pharmacy: is a prescription needed, how often is it taken, how is it used. The second uses the verb of permission, because the question means 'am I allowed to'. First, eight words.
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün telefonda konuşmayı öğren: Hello! Today we will learn to speak on the phone: introducing yourself, asking for somebody and saying you will ring back. On the phone there is no face, so the patterns matter all the more. Ready?
lecture.Aksilik anlatırken kuralsız ortaçlar yin: Irregular participles turn up again when you tell of a mishap; one of today's verbs is irregular, separable and a verb of change of place all at once, so three rules together. First, eight words.
lecture.Almancada bunun hazır kalıpları var ve h: German has ready patterns for this and all of them use the soft form of the verb. Say it outright and a row starts; say it in the soft form and the conversation opens. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün insanları tarif etmeyi öğ: Hello! Today we will learn to describe people: 'the woman sitting next to me', 'the child who asks a lot of questions'. German does this with a subclause and that clause comes AFTER the noun. Ready?
lecture.Türkçede soru sormak için sona küçük bir: English has no such ending either; it moves the verb to the front, and German does the same. An invitation is built in exactly that way. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Abonelik konuşmalarının üç sorusu var: n: A conversation about a contract has three questions: how much, for how long, what is included. The comparative helps with the first and adjectives of frequency with the second. First, eight words.
lecture.Sayıları biliyorsun, şimdi onları kullan: You know the numbers, now we will use them. In English you say 'I am thirty' and two words are enough; in German you have to add two more words beside the number. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.İyelik kelimesinin dişilde uzadığını bil: You know that the possessive word gets longer in the feminine. Today the same rule will hold for two new words: 'our' and 'her'. The rule does not change, only the word does. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Kural cümlelerinde Türkçe 'yapılmaz' der: In English a rule is said in the passive — 'that is not done' — and it does not say who does not do it. German has a special word for it: a subject that points at nobody and covers everybody. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Merhaba! Almanya'da yeni tanıştığın biri: Hello! One of the first things somebody you have just met in Germany will ask you is your hobby. Today we will learn to say what you do in your free time and what you enjoy doing. Are you ready to start?
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün bir festivali anlatacağız: Hello! Today we will describe a festival. In accounts like this German uses noun phrases instead of subclauses: not 'while the band was on stage' but 'during the band's performance'. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Modülün son dersi. Bugün resmî: Hello! The module's last lesson. Today a small but unmistakable mark of formal German: some prepositions want the genitive. Using them correctly in speech gives your level away at once. Ready?
lecture.Almancada fiilin sonu kişiye göre değişi: In German the ending of the verb changes with the person — far more than in English. 'I work' ends in e, 'you work' ends in st. This verb's stem ends in t, so another e slips in between:
lecture.Bir anıyı anlatırken iki şey iç içe geçe: Two things run together when you tell a memory: what happened and how you felt at the time. The event is built with the Perfekt and the feeling with the short past of the verb to be. Today we will use both together.
lecture.Küçük ve geçici bir yerde iyi tarafları: In a small and temporary place you have to bring the good sides forward; for that we will use the conjunction of reservation. You saw it in the work module and here we will work it at home. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün zevk üzerine konuşacağız: Hello! Today we will talk about taste — and an argument about taste has one rule: nobody convinces anybody. So we will learn both to compare and to end the argument. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Bugünkü ders küçük bir kelimeye: Hello! Today's lesson looks at a little word but it changes the meaning completely. In English 'the door is being opened' and 'the door is open' are quite different things; German separates them with two different passives. Ready?
lecture.Merhaba! Modülün son dersi ve konusu key: Hello! The module's last lesson and its subject is a pleasant one: expensive hobbies. But the grammar is serious — we will build the possessive relative clause once more, this time watching the agreement of the verb. Ready?
lecture.Yani 'Sen bunu nasıl buluyorsun?' Bu fii: That is, 'How do you find it?' You used this verb in the supermarket when you asked where you find something; here it asks for an opinion about something. In English we say 'how do you find it' too — the same verb, the same logic.
lecture.Yani 'Diş macununa ihtiyacım var'. Türkç: That is, 'I need toothpaste'. In English the noun does not change at all; in German the noun stays the same too but the little word in front of it can change — though with feminine and neuter words that does not change either.
lecture.Bir hedef söylenirken kararlı niyet bild: When you state a goal the modal of firm intention is used; the polite form of wishing is too weak here. When a time phrase comes with it, that phrase goes into the accusative. First, eight words.
lecture.Mantığı şu: iki olaydan hangisinin daha: The logic is this: to show which of two events came first, the earlier one is pulled one layer further back. The auxiliary itself goes into its past form too. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Şimdi tarih. Türkçede 'bir mayıs' dersin: Now the date. English turns the day number into an ordinal too — 'the first of May' — and German does the same: first, second, third. And the preposition we use for days comes at the front.
lecture.Almanya'da hayır demek kabalık sayılmaz;: Saying no is not counted rude in Germany; what is rude is leaving the answer unclear. But there is a three-part order: say you are sorry, say why, offer a new day. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Bir haftayı özetlemek tek tek olayları s: Summing up a week is not listing the events one by one; it is saying which of them is finished and which of them came off. Three of today's verbs are separable and their participles open up in the middle again.
lecture.Bugün randevu almayı öğreneceğiz: gün ön: Today we will learn to make an appointment: proposing a day, discussing the time and putting it back if you have to. You remember that one word is used for days and another for times; today we will work it. Ready?
lecture.İki fiil geçmişte Perfekt'e girmez: olma: Two verbs do not go into the Perfekt in the past: to be and to have. They have short past forms of their own and this is the past you hear most in speech. Today we will work them with eight new words.
lecture.Almanya'da toplu taşıma dakikası dakikas: Public transport in Germany runs to the minute, so everybody says clearly which way they travel. There is one little word for it and that word is the heart of this lesson. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Haber aktarırken iki şey birden söylenir: Two things are said at once when you pass news on: who you heard it from and what you heard. The second comes as a subclause and the verb goes last. And a short pattern is used for questioning a piece of news. First, eight words.
lecture.Yani 'Hangi bedeni giyiyorsunuz?' Türkçe: That is, 'What size do you take?' In English we ask 'what size do you take'; German uses the verb 'to have'. Do not try to translate it word for word, take the pattern as it stands. Your answer is very short too: a number.
lecture.Bugünkü fiillerin bir kısmı kuralsız ort: Some of today's verbs build an irregular participle and some do something of their own: verbs starting with an unstressed prefix take no participle syllable at all. You will see this in two words at once.
lecture.Türkçede edilgen fiile bir ek getirerek: English builds the passive with an auxiliary too — 'it is paid', 'it is calculated'. German does the same: a separate auxiliary comes in and the past form of the main verb drops to the end of the sentence. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Bir deneyimi anlatmak üç parçadan oluşur: Telling of an experience has three parts: what you tried, what it was like at the start and what you thought at the end. The first is built with the past tense, the second and third with the short past of the verb to be. First, eight words.
lecture.Bu derste bir cümleyi olduğu gibi ezberl: In this lesson we will learn one sentence exactly as it stands: the one that says you are lost. We will look at the tense inside it separately later on; for now use it as a ready phrase. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Fark ettin mi: yatak odası ve oturma oda: Did you notice: the bedroom and the living room take the same article. Because both end in the word for room and the article always comes from the last part. The kitchen and the hall carry articles of their own.
lecture.Kadeh kaldırırken kimin şerefine olduğun: When you raise a glass a preposition is used to say whose health it is, and that preposition brings the accusative. And when you give an opinion a subclause is built and the verb goes to the end again. First, eight words.
lecture.Kural tek cümle: ön ek başta kalır, orta: The rule is one sentence: the prefix stays at the front, the participle syllable goes in between the prefix and the stem, and the whole thing is written as one word. All eight of today's verbs are separable; you will see the same thing in all eight.
lecture.Taşınma hikâyesinde iki tür fiil bir ara: Two kinds of verb stand together in a story about moving: those of change of place take the first auxiliary and the rest take the second. Today's two separable verbs show exactly this distinction. First, eight words.
lecture.Türkçede soruyu olduğu gibi gömersin: 'n: In English you embed the question and the order turns into statement order: 'I know where it is'. German embeds it too but one thing changes — the question word becomes a conjunction and the verb drops to the end of the sentence. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Resmî bir yazı Almancada belirli bir hit: A formal letter in German starts with a set greeting and the adjective in that greeting takes its ending from the gender of the person you write to. This pattern is always the same in a letter, an email and an application; it is learnt by heart. First, eight words.
lecture.Resmî yerlerde hep kibar biçim kullanılı: At an office the polite form is always used and the questions are always the same; learn them by heart and you will never struggle again. And there is a small trap: German asks for a name with 'how', not 'what'. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Türkçede 'çarşamba günü saat onda' dersi: In English you say 'on Wednesday at ten o'clock' with two different prepositions, and German splits them in the very same way: one preposition for the day, another for the time, and swapping them breaks the sentence. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Yani 'İyi yüzerim'. Cümlenin şekline dik: That is, 'I swim well'. Mind the shape of the sentence: the verb of being able stands in second place and the main verb waits at the very end. English keeps the main verb right after the modal, so this order will need getting used to.
lecture.Edilgen çatıyı biliyorsun. Bugün onun üs: You know the passive. Today we will put a layer on top of it: used together with obligation it comes out as 'it needs repairing', and both verbs go to the end at once. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Bu derste küçük ama şart olan bir kelime: There is a small but obligatory word in this lesson. English cannot leave the subject empty either — you say 'it is raining' — and German puts a ready subject into weather sentences in the same way. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Türkçede 'benim' hep aynı kalır: benim a: In English 'my' always stays the same: my mother, my father. In German this word looks at what stands beside it and gets a letter longer in front of a feminine word. That little letter is our real business today. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Türkçede 'bir kardeşim var' derken 'bir': In English the 'a' never changes: I have a brother. In German, when you say you have something, that thing becomes the object of the sentence, and as an object masculine words change form. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Umut, düşünce ve haber bildiren fiillerd: After verbs of hoping, thinking and reporting a subclause follows and in that clause the verb goes to the very end. You saw this rule in module 5; here we will work it in an everyday conversation about plans. First, eight words.
lecture.Bir ayrım var ve Türkçede yok: kişinin k: There is a distinction and English has it too: for a quality of the person you use 'to be', for something on you or on your body 'to have'. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Bu soru Almanya'da tanıştıktan beş dakik: This question always comes five minutes after meeting somebody in Germany. And we will learn a new question form: English moves the verb to the front, and German does exactly the same. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Bugünkü iki fiil kuralsız ve ikisi de or: Both of today's verbs are irregular and neither takes the participle syllable, because they start with an unstressed prefix. The present and the participle look almost the same; the auxiliary makes the difference. First, eight words.
lecture.Şimdi dikkat: rengi kelimenin önüne koym: Now mind this: putting the colour in front of the word makes it harder. Saying 'a red jacket' gives the colour an ending and those endings are too early for now. Luckily nobody in a shop talks like that; everybody uses this little trick:
lecture.Şimdi kuralı görelim. Cümleye normalde ö: Now let us see the rule. Normally you start the sentence with the subject. But if you put a time phrase at the front, that phrase becomes the first element and the verb throws the subject behind it to keep its own place. So the subject and the verb change places.
lecture.Bir önceki derste olmak ve sahip olmak f: In the last lesson you saw the short past of to be and to have. Now we will use them with a negative: saying 'there was not' means the past of to have plus a negative. First, eight words.
lecture.Burada küçük ama önemli bir ayrım var. T: There is a small but important distinction here. In English 'very expensive' can be said with admiration; the word in this pattern means 'more than it should be'. So when you build this sentence the seller understands that you will not buy it.
lecture.Burada yeni bir kural yok; ağrı kalıbı,: There is no new rule here; the pattern for pain, the pattern for appointments and the pattern for obligation come together. The only new thing is the doctor's short instructions: understanding them is enough, you do not have to build them. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Pazarlığın kibar hâli bir soruyla açılır: The polite form of bargaining opens with a question and that question uses the comparative: 'could it be a bit cheaper'. Pointing in a direction rather than naming a price outright is more courteous in German. First, eight words.
lecture.Bu derste iki hâl yan yana duruyor: karg: Two cases stand side by side in this lesson: the person RECEIVING the parcel in the dative, the parcel ITSELF in the accusative. And there is a preposition that says on whose behalf you take it, and it brings the accusative. First, eight words.
lecture.Koşul cümlesini bu modülde bir kez daha: We will use the conditional clause once more in this module, but this time with a feeling: if I am nervous, this happens. And the verb for sitting an exam is a separable one, with its prefix dropping to the end of the sentence. First, eight words.
lecture.Bankada sorular hep soru kelimesiyle baş: At the bank the questions always start with a question word, and one of them is interesting: the 'how much' question is built not from one word but from a question word joined to an adjective — English does the same with 'how high'. First, eight words.
lecture.Bu bağlaç iki parçalıdır: birincisi ilk: This conjunction has two parts: the first stands in front of the first option, the second in front of the second. It does exactly the same job as the English 'either … or'. Today we take the first of them into the glossary. First, eight words.
lecture.Özür kalıbında üzülen kişi özne değil, y: In a pattern of apology the person who is sorry is not the subject but stands in the dative; the subject of the sentence is an impersonal word. A subclause follows and there the auxiliary of the past goes to the very end. First, eight words.
lecture.Türkçede olumsuzluk fiilin içine girer:: In English the negative is a separate word too, but it stays beside the verb: I do not understand. In German it is a separate word as well and it is usually thrown to the end of the sentence. Get its place wrong and the sentence falls apart; luckily the rule is simple. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Şimdi üç fiil. Ayakları üstünde duran eş: Now three verbs. One is used for things standing on their feet, another for things lying flat, a third for things hanging on the wall. And there is this too: when you say where something is, the article of the word changes.
lecture.Merhaba! Bugün cümleleri sonuçla bağlaya: Hello! Today we will link sentences with a result: 'There was traffic, that is why I was late.' In German deshalb, darum and deswegen are the same thing; all of them follow one rule: they take first place and the verb comes right after. Ready?
lecture.Bu derste küçük bir kelime var ki bütün: There is a little word in this lesson that is the key to every conversation about free time. In English we use a separate verb, 'I like'; German adds one single word to the sentence without touching the verb. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Resepsiyonda kullanılan sorular soru kel: The questions used at a reception start with a question word and some of them join up with a preposition: 'from when', 'until when'. The preposition stands right at the front and the question word comes after it. First, eight words.
lecture.Türkçede 'göl var' deriz ve tek kelime y: In English 'there is a lake' needs two words, and German uses a ready two-word pattern for it as well; what follows the pattern counts as an object. That detail is the crux of the lesson. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Ve bu A2'nin son dersiydi. Yüz derste ge: And that was A2's last lesson. In a hundred lessons you have learnt to tell the past, to build subclauses, to tell the cases apart and to speak in every scene of daily life. Now look back and say in your own sentences what you can do.
lecture.Gelecek zaman Almancada iki iş görür: ta: The future does two jobs in German: forecasting and deciding. When you say your own plan it states a decision, and that sounds firmer than saying it in the present. The auxiliary in second place, the main verb last. First, eight words.
lecture.Meslek adları Almancada bir kalıba oturu: The names of professions follow a pattern in German: the masculine form is the base and the feminine takes an ending. No article comes when a profession is named. The reason is added with a subclause and there the verb goes last. First, eight words.
lecture.Tanıtma fiili iki nesne alıyor: tanıtıla: The verb of introducing takes two objects: the person introduced in the accusative, the person they are introduced to in the dative. The order you worked on in module 4 holds here too. In a formal setting the polite address is always used. First, eight words.
lecture.Ağrı anlatmanın iki yolu var, ikisi de d: There are two ways of describing pain and both are right. One is just like English, the other not at all, and yet Germans mostly use the second in everyday speech. We will learn both. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Geçmiş zamanda soru sorarken yardımcı fi: When you ask a question in the past the auxiliary moves to the front and the participle stays at the end. With a separable verb the participle syllable again sits between the prefix and the stem. This is the sentence built most while packing a case. First, eight words.
lecture.Şimdi kural. Bu fiillerin başındaki küçü: Now the rule. The little piece at the front of these verbs does not stay put once a sentence is built: the stem of the verb moves into second place and the front piece goes to the very end. So the verb splits in two and embraces the sentence.
lecture.Bir kip fiili ile dönüşlü fiil aynı cüml: When a modal and a reflexive verb are in the same sentence the pronoun stays where it is: right after the modal. The main verb goes to the end but the pronoun does not travel with it. This is one of the orders that gets confused most. First, eight words.
lecture.Almancada fiilin sonu her kişide değişir: In German the ending of the verb changes with every person and the subject is never dropped. English never drops it either — you always say 'I come' — so that part will be familiar. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Yani 'Dosdoğru gidin'. Türkçede emir eki: That is, 'Go straight on'. In English the imperative has no pronoun at all: you simply say 'go'. In German the verb jumps to the front of the sentence and 'Sie' is put right behind it. Without the person named it is not an imperative.
That is, 'I would like to exchange the trousers'. Mind the end of the sentence: with two verbs the second goes to the very end. English puts the object after the second verb, so this will need getting used to.
lecture.Bugünkü sıfatların dördü de ortaçtan gel: All four of today's adjectives come from participles: the participle of a verb has come to be used as an adjective. That is why they all end in the same syllables and all carry the sense of 'something happened and this is the result'. First, eight words.
lecture.Koşul cümlesinde fiil en sona gider ve k: In the conditional clause the verb goes to the very end, and when the condition comes first the subject in the main clause falls behind the verb. Today we will use this pattern together with a reflexive verb, so the pronoun joins the queue in the main clause too. First, eight words.
lecture.Resmî bildirimde yan cümle kullanılır: ': A formal notice uses a subclause: 'I have to tell you that I am ill'. This sounds natural in English too and in German it is the standard. And we will learn the words for email; putting the certificate in the right place is half the process. First, eight words.
lecture.Ayrım şu: bir yerden bir yere gitmeyi an: The distinction is this: verbs of going from one place to another and verbs of changing state take a different auxiliary. The rest is as before. This group is small but the verbs you use most are in it. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Bir hayat hikâyesinde iki zaman iç içe g: Two tenses run together in a life story: how it was in the past and how it is today. For the past we will use the short forms of to be and to have; for today, the plain present. First, eight words.
lecture.Bugünkü bağlaç bir düşünceyi ya da bir i: Today's conjunction puts a thought or a wish inside a sentence. In English you say 'we want it to be clean' with an infinitive; German brings a separate conjunction and the verb drops to the end again. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Bunun için bir bağlaç var ve Türkçedeki: There is a conjunction for it and it works like the English 'although'. But there is a difference: in German the conjunction goes to the front of its clause and throws the verb to the end of it. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.İltifat kalıplarında iltifat edilen kişi: In patterns of compliment the person complimented is not the subject but stands in the dative. The subject of the sentence is the garment or the quality itself. The same structure as the English 'that suits you': not 'you' but 'to you'. First, eight words.
lecture.İki şeyin arasını anlatan edat, öteki ik: The preposition that says what lies between two things works like the other two-case prepositions, but with a difference: it takes two nouns at once and both go into the same case. If it answers the question WHERE, both are in the dative. First, eight words.
lecture.Resmî emirde fiil başa geçer ve hitap za: In a formal imperative the verb moves to the front and the address pronoun stays right behind it; in the familiar one the pronoun would be dropped. If the verb is separable the prefix goes to the end of the sentence. These three things appear together constantly on forms. First, eight words.
lecture.Bu görüşmede sebep bildirmek merkezî: he: Giving reasons is central to this interview: every assessment has grounds behind it and you are expected to give yours with grounds too. We will use the conjunction from the module's second lesson here in a work setting. First, eight words.
lecture.Katılmak fiili kendi edatını taşır ve o: The verb for taking part carries its own preposition and that preposition brings the dative; it is a separable verb as well. And we will work the future once more in this lesson: the auxiliary in second place, the main verb last. First, eight words.
lecture.Samimi hitapta emir kurmak kolay: fiilin: Building an imperative in the familiar form is easy: take the verb as conjugated for the person you are talking to and drop the pronoun. If the verb is separable the prefix goes to the end of the sentence. In English a phrasal verb can split too — 'turn it off' — and in German the prefix travels right to the end. First, eight words.
lecture.Geçen ders yan cümle baştaydı ve ana cüm: Last lesson the subclause came first and the order of the main clause was broken. Put the subclause second and the main clause does not change at all; only the subclause keeps its own verb at the end. So the shift of order depends on where the subclause stands. First, eight words.
lecture.Kuralı çok kısa: karşındaki için çektiği: The rule is very short: take the verb as conjugated for the person you are talking to, drop the last two letters and do not say the subject. What is left is the imperative. In English too the imperative is the barest form of the verb, so the logic will not feel foreign. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.A1'de bir şeyi sevdiğini söylemeyi öğren: At A1 you learnt to say that you like something. Today its comparative form comes: with two options it says which you prefer. There is a superlative too and that picks one out of them all. First, eight words.
lecture.Mahalle anlatırken kullandığın edatların: Almost all the prepositions you use to describe your area want a single case: the dative. These are not like the two-case prepositions, they always bring the same case; that is good news, because you have no decision to make. First, eight words.
lecture.Türkçede 'insan şunu yapmalı' deriz ve k: In English we say 'one should do this' and mean nobody in particular. German has an indefinite subject of its own for it and the verb always stays singular. Joined to the soft form of the modal it makes a courteous piece of general advice. First, eight words.
lecture.Ayrım şu: bir durumdaysan 'olmak' fiilin: The distinction is this: if you are in a state you use the verb 'to be', if you have something on you the verb 'to have'. English needs two different verbs as well: 'I am ill' and 'I have a cold' — German does exactly the same. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.En kritik ayrım şu: izin fiilinin olumsu: The most critical distinction is this: the negative of the verb of permission does not mean 'no need', it means 'forbidden'. The negative of the verb of obligation really does mean 'no need'. Mixing the two means understanding the exact opposite of what the doctor said. First, eight words.
lecture.Geçen derste doktorun ağzından katı bir: In the last lesson you saw hard advice in the doctor's mouth. The same modal has a soft form too, and you use it when you give a friend advice. Like the difference in English between 'you should drink' and 'you must drink'. First, eight words.
lecture.Kural aynı: koşul cümlesinde fiil sonda,: The rule is the same: in the conditional clause the verb is last, and with the condition first the subject in the main clause stands behind the verb. The only thing that changes is the form of address. In the polite form the imperative is built differently too: the verb goes to the front but the pronoun is not dropped. First, eight words.
lecture.A1'de kibar bir istek biçimi öğrenmiştin: At A1 you learnt a polite way of wanting: I would like a coffee, I would like to go. Today its firmer sibling comes. Both state an intention but one is a request and the other a decision. In a work conversation the firm one is used. First, eight words.
lecture.Tarih söylerken sayı bir sıra sayısına d: When you give a date the number turns into an ordinal and a fused preposition comes in front of it. English turns the day number into an ordinal too — 'the third of May' — and German does the same, with the ordinal taking an ending and going into the dative. First, eight words.
lecture.Yani 'Kazak ne kadar?' Bu soruyu büfede: That is, 'How much is the jumper?' You heard this question at the snack stand; now it will help you in a shop too. In English we usually ask 'how much is it'; German has a verb of its own for it and the question starts with the word 'what'.
lecture.Kararlı niyet bildiren kip fiilini bu mo: You saw the modal of firm intention in this module's first lesson. Here we will use it together with a date. And we will learn four words about time; these are the backbone of conversations about leave and appointments. First, eight words.
lecture.Reddin üç parçası var: üzüntü, sebep ve: A refusal has three parts: regret, a reason and an alternative. The reason is said in a subclause and there the modal goes to the very end, with the main verb right in front of it. This double order is one of the things most often confused at A2. First, eight words.
lecture.Yani 'Otobüsle gidiyorum'. Türkçede arac: That is, 'I go by bus'. English puts a preposition in front — by bus, by tube — and the noun does not change. German does not change the noun either; what changes is the little word in front of it after the preposition of travel. With masculine and neuter vehicles
lecture.Türkçede sıfat hiç değişmez: büyük oda,: In English an adjective never changes: a big room, in the big room, the big room. In German the adjective takes an ending from the article in front of it and from the case of the noun. The rule looks complicated but a few forms will do for everyday speech. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Yardım edilen kişi Almancada belirtme hâ: The person being helped stands in German not in the accusative but in the dative. In English you say 'help me' with a plain object, so most learners try to build this verb the same way in German — and that is exactly the mistake. First, eight words.
lecture.Hediye eden fiiller iki nesne alır: hedi: Verbs of giving take two objects: the person receiving the present in the dative, the present itself in the accusative. The order is the same too: the person first, the thing after. We will work this rule, familiar from module 4, here in a setting of celebration. First, eight words.
lecture.Resepsiyonun soruları hep soru kelimesiy: The reception's questions always start with a question word and in questions of that kind the verb stands in second place. When a question word joins a preposition the preposition comes first and the question word after it — in English the preposition comes first too, 'since when', so this part will look familiar. First, eight words.
lecture.Yani 'Severek futbol oynarım'. Dikkat et: That is, 'I like playing football'. Mind this: in German we do not build a separate verb 'to like' as English does. The verb stays the same, one single word is added after it and the meaning becomes 'I enjoy doing it'. Whichever verb you attach this word to it does the same job.
lecture.Türkçede 'tren gecikmeli' deriz, yani bi: In English we say 'the train is delayed', that is, we use an adjective. In German the delay is something the train has: 'the train has delay'. That is why the verb here is not 'to be' but 'to have'. And that is exactly where the common mistake is made.
lecture.En üstünlük iki parçadan oluşuyor: sıfat: The superlative is made of two pieces: a fused preposition in front of the adjective and a syllable at the end. Together they give the sense of 'the most … of all'. English marks it at both ends too — 'the cheapest' — and German does the same. First, eight words.
lecture.Yani 'Bir kazak arıyorum'. Burada küçük: That is, 'I am looking for a jumper'. There is a small rule here that will be very useful. In English neither the noun nor the word in front of it changes; in German the noun does not change either but the little word in front of it does. Its dictionary form
lecture.Bugünkü fiillerin üçü İngilizceden gelmi: Three of today's verbs have come from English and been taken into German conjugation: they take German endings and their participles are built by the German rule. This is a good example of how a language takes new words in. First, eight words.
lecture.Türkçesi 'Bu hoşuma gitti'. Şimdi güzel: It means 'I like this'. Now the tricky part: in English the person who likes is the subject — 'I like it'. German works the other way round: the thing liked is the subject and the person stands behind. So do not try to build 'I like'; build 'it is pleasing to me'.
lecture.Kalıp şu: kendine zarar verdiğini söyler: The pattern is this: when you say you have hurt yourself the reflexive pronoun stands in the dative and the definite article is used in front of the part that got hurt. In English you say 'I hurt my wrist' with a possessive; German says 'I hurt myself the wrist'. First, eight words.
lecture.Bu kip fiili 'benim zorunluluğum' demez;: This modal does not say 'my obligation'; it says 'somebody else said so'. You use exactly this when you carry the doctor's advice home. It is what English adds with 'I am supposed to drink it'. First, eight words.
lecture.Kuaförde istekler hep karşılaştırma biçi: At the hairdresser's requests are always said with the comparative, because you give not a measure but a direction: shorter than it is now. And when something is done to a person that person goes into the dative; you saw that in module 3 as well. First, eight words.
lecture.Bir yeri geçmişte anlatırken en çok kull: The pattern used most for describing a place in the past is 'there was'. German has a form of its own for it and the noun that follows goes into the accusative. Today we will work it together with the short past of the verb to be. First, eight words.
lecture.Bu kip fiilinin ilginç bir kullanımı var: This modal has an interesting use: together with an expression of direction the main verb is not said at all. In 'you have to go to the security check' the verb 'to go' drops away, because it is understood. English has no such shortening. First, eight words.
lecture.Aynı anlamı iki yolla söyleyebilirsin: f: You can say the same thing in two ways: with a verb or with a noun. Their prepositions are DIFFERENT and this is one of the things that surprises you while learning German. With the verb one preposition comes, with the noun another, and their cases differ too. First, eight words.
lecture.Beğeni bildiren fiil Almancada ilginç ça: The verb of liking works in an interesting way in German: the thing liked is the subject and the person liking stands in the dative. It is the opposite of the English 'I like it'. Joined to the superlative it comes out as 'I like this one best'. First, eight words.
lecture.Beklemek fiili Almancada hep aynı edatı: The verb for waiting always takes the same preposition in German and that preposition brings the accusative. English uses a preposition here too — to wait for — but not the same one, so the German preposition is learnt together with the verb. First, eight words.
lecture.Sır şu: Türkçede tek bir çoğul eki vardı: The secret is this: in English the plural is nearly always an -s with a handful of exceptions. German has five separate ways and which one comes cannot be predicted; that is why the plural is learnt together with the word. It sounds like bad news but that is the whole of it. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Türkçede her yere aynı ekle gideriz: den: In English we use different words for different places too: to the seaside, into the mountains, to the city. German has three separate prepositions and all of them bring the accusative, because movement is involved. Names of cities and countries take a preposition of their own. We will see this through the module. First, eight words.
lecture.Kültür karşılaştırması iki araç istiyor:: Comparing cultures wants two tools: the comparative and the indefinite subject. With the first you say 'here it is more …', with the second 'here it is done this way'. Both are structures you have learnt at this level; here they work side by side. First, eight words.
lecture.Aitlik fiili Almancada beklenmedik bir ş: The verb of belonging does something unexpected in German: the owner is not the subject but an object in the dative. In English we say 'this is mine' and 'mine' stands like a predicate; German says 'this belongs to me'. The question word carries that case's own form too. First, eight words.
lecture.Talimatlar hep aynı biçimde gelir. Türkç: Instructions always come in the same shape. In English the imperative is the bare verb: 'take'. In German the verb goes right to the front of the sentence and the polite address comes straight after it. Once you know this shape you will see it on every sign and in every set of instructions. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Arıza bildirirken iki kalıp yeter: neyin: Two patterns are enough for reporting a fault: saying what is broken and asking for somebody to be sent. In the second two objects come side by side — to you and somebody — and the order you have worked on all module holds here too: the person first, the thing after. First, eight words.
lecture.Günlük konuşmada geçmiş iki parçalı kuru: In everyday speech the past is built in two pieces, as you know. But in a CV, in formal correspondence and in the serious part of a job interview a one-piece form is used. With regular verbs the rule is simple: a short ending goes onto the stem. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Cümlede iki nesne var: verilen şey ve al: There are two objects in the sentence: the thing given and the person receiving. In English the receiver takes a different pronoun form: me, you, him. German changes the case too and the pronouns carry separate forms for it. The order matters as well: the receiver comes BEFORE the thing given. First, eight words.
lecture.Duyguyu söylerken Almancada ilginç bir ş: Something interesting happens in German when you say the feeling: the person who is embarrassed sits not in the subject but in the dative. The same logic as the English 'it was very embarrassing for me'. Today we will work it together with an irregular verb and a reflexive verb. First, eight words.
lecture.Mesaj iletirken geçen dersteki bağlaç yi: When you pass a message on the conjunction from the last lesson turns up again: telling somebody that you will say something builds a subclause and the verb goes last. Three things happen at once in this sentence: the person told in the dative, the conjunction in the middle, the verb at the end. First, eight words.
lecture.Postanede üç şey konuşulur: ne kadar ağı: Three things are discussed at the post office: how heavy, how much it costs, how long it takes. The third uses the superlative. And the units of weight: in German these always stay singular after a number, which is not what English does. First, eight words.
lecture.Perfekt iki parçadan oluşur: yardımcı fi: The Perfekt is made of two pieces: the auxiliary in second place and the main verb as a participle at the end of the sentence. The auxiliary is not always the same; verbs of change of place take one and the rest the other. Three of today's eight words carry exactly that distinction. The words first.
lecture.Bir ülkede neyin olduğunu anlatırken 'va: When you say what there is in a country the 'there is' pattern is used and the noun that follows goes into the accusative. When you describe a general custom the indefinite subject is used and the verb always stays singular. The two together are the most practical way of describing a culture. First, eight words.
lecture.Rehberler geçmişi anlatırken Perfekt değ: Guides do not use the Perfekt when they tell the past; they use the short forms. You saw to be and to have in module 1; in an account of a city they will come up constantly. And we will learn a pattern for saying how old a building is. First, eight words.
lecture.Türkçede sıra çoğu zaman fiilin kendisin: In English we use separate words for the order too — first, then, after that — but the subject stays in front of the verb. In German these words push the subject behind the verb when they come to the front of the sentence. Today we will see both the words and that change of places.
lecture.Türkçede zorunluluk fiilin içine girer:: In English the job is split as well — 'I have to go' is two words. In German the finite verb settles into second place and the main verb is thrown to the very end in the infinitive. That habit of throwing things to the end is German's signature. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Birinci yol dönüşlü fiil: kendini iyi ya: The first way is a reflexive verb: feeling well or feeling ill. The second is more interesting: with symptoms like dizziness or nausea the person is not the subject but stands in the dative. Rather like saying 'I feel sick' instead of 'my head is turning'. First, eight words.
lecture.Kurallar iki biçimde söylenir: sana özel: Rules are stated in two ways: with the verb of permission and a person when it is about you, and with the indefinite subject when it holds for everybody. In the second the verb always stays singular. You saw the verb of permission in module 3 and the indefinite subject in module 8; here they come together. First, eight words.
lecture.Koşul cümlesinde fiil en sona gider ve k: In the conditional clause the verb goes to the very end, and with the condition first the subject in the main clause falls behind the verb. In English neither of these happens — the verb keeps its place in both halves — so in German two things change at once. First, eight words.
lecture.Yani 'Burada ne görülebilir?' Türkçede b: That is, 'What can you see here?' In English we put in a 'you' or a 'one'; German cannot leave the subject empty either and uses a little word that means everybody at once. The thing to be seen is named and then the verb goes to the very end.
lecture.Aradaki fark şu: bir şeyi başka bir hâle: The difference is this: turning something into something else, as against giving one thing up and taking another. Move the time of your appointment and it is the first; leave your doctor for another one and it is the second. In English we say 'change' for both, so they are easy to confuse. First, eight words.
lecture.Fark tek cümlede: bugünkü bağlaçtan sonr: The difference is one sentence: after today's conjunction the sentence is built normally and the verb stays in second place. After last lesson's conjunction the verb went to the very end. The meaning is the same in both; which you choose is up to you, but the moment you choose it the word order is settled. First, eight words.
lecture.İki adım var. Birincisi sıfatın sonuna g: There are two steps. The first is the ending that goes onto the adjective; with most short adjectives the middle vowel changes as well. The second is the word of comparison: it does the job of the English 'than' and stands between the two things. Today we take that word into the glossary too. First, eight words.
lecture.Türkçede 'üç yıldır buradayım' ve 'üç yı: In English 'I have been here for three years' and 'I came three years ago' use two different words. German has two different prepositions and both put the noun after them into the dative. The one for duration works with the present, the one for a point in time with the past. First, eight words.
lecture.Bugünkü bağlaç, düşünme ve söyleme fiill: Today's conjunction comes after verbs of thinking and saying: I think that, I hope that, she says that. In English 'that' exists but is usually dropped; in German it can be left out as well, and yet we will build it throughout this lesson, because the rule lives in the place of the verb. First, eight words.
lecture.Türkçede 'bol su içmeli' dersin ve kimin: In English you have to say 'one should drink plenty of water' or 'you should'; German never leaves the subject empty either and puts in a little word that means everybody. You met that word in the lesson on spelling; today we will use it together with the pattern of obligation. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Türkçede sıfat hiç değişmez: yeşil ceket: In English an adjective never changes: a green jacket, a green shirt, green shoes. In German the adjective takes a letter at the end according to the gender of the noun. Today we are working its easiest form: after an indefinite article. With eight colours and patterns you will see the same rule eight times. The words first.
lecture.Bugün aynı zamanda bir alışkanlık kuraca: Today we will also build a habit. In English you say 'head' and that is that; in German the little word in front of the word is part of the word. A word learnt without it is only half learnt. Three of today's five take a different article, which makes it a proper exercise. Let us learn the words first.
lecture.Aynı edatlar, başka hâl: hareket varsa,: The same prepositions, a different case: if there is movement, that is, if something is going somewhere, the preposition brings the accusative. Two little words will help you today as well: one shows movement away from the speaker, the other towards them. In English both are covered by 'there' and 'here'. First, eight words.
lecture.Şikâyeti yumuşatmanın iki yolu var. Biri: There are two ways of softening a complaint. The first is a conditional clause: instead of accusing, saying 'when this happens, that happens'. The second is the polite form of the modal. In the conditional clause the verb goes to the very end; we will study that rule in detail in module 9 and use it here as a set phrase. First, eight words.
lecture.Yani 'Maalesef gelemiyorum'. Bunu randev: That is, 'I am afraid I cannot'. You may remember this from the lesson on appointments; today we go into it properly. Because you started the sentence with the word of regret the verb moved right behind it and you dropped into third place. In German the verb always stands in second place, and this sentence is a fine example of that.
lecture.Bugünkü bağlaç bir yan cümle açar ve o y: Today's conjunction opens a subclause and in that clause the verb goes to the VERY END. In English the verb does not go last, so this rule wants practice; and the harder part is that the verb of the main clause still stays in second place. We will also see a way of giving a reason with a single preposition. First, eight words.
lecture.Almancada bazı fiiller yanlarında küçük: In German some verbs carry a little pronoun beside them. English usually has no counterpart for it: we say 'we met' and there is no word in between. In German the sentence cannot be built without it and it changes with the person. With two people the same pronoun means 'each other'. First, eight words.
lecture.Kural iki parçalı. Birincisi: yan cümled: The rule has two parts. First: in the subclause the verb goes to the very end. Second: if the subclause comes first the subject in the main clause falls behind the verb. In English neither of these happens — the verb keeps its place in both halves. In German two things change at once. First, eight words.
lecture.Bir dönemi özetlerken sekiz küçük kelime: Eight little words will do when you sum up a period: almost, even, at least, besides. These carry not the meaning of the sentence but its tone, and they turn an account from a flat list into an assessment. Their place in German is fixed and put in the wrong place the sentence sounds odd. First, eight words.
lecture.'Var' kalıbı Almancada beklenmedik biçim: The 'there is' pattern is built unexpectedly in German: an impersonal subject and the verb 'to give'. Word for word it means 'it gives', but its sense is 'there is'. The noun that follows counts not as the subject but as the object and goes into the accusative. This is one of the patterns English speakers get wrong most. First, eight words.
lecture.Almancada gelecek çoğu zaman şimdiki zam: In German the future is usually said with the present; a word like tomorrow or next week is enough. But when you make a forecast a separate auxiliary is used and the main verb goes to the end. A weather forecast is where this is used most naturally. And the subject of weather sentences is always that same impersonal word. First, eight words.
lecture.Türkçede geçmiş eki hep aynıdır: geldim,: In English there is a group of verbs that change in the past: came, went, ate. German has the same group, and its irregular verbs change both their ending and their middle vowel when they build a participle. There is no rule, they are learnt by heart; but the good news is that they are the verbs used most, so you will hear them every day and pick them up by themselves. lecture.Bazı edatlar iki hâl birden alabilir. Ha: Some prepositions can take two cases.
