task.explanation.tr\u0000Bir işi NİÇİN yaptığ: When you say WHY you do something and both halves have the SAME subject, you use „um … zu“. It is what English does with "in order to".
task.explanation.tr\u0000İkinci yarının öznes: If the second half has a different subject, „um … zu“ is impossible and you need „damit“. „damit“ opens a subordinate clause, so the finite verb goes to the end.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Genelde fail hiç söy: Usually the agent is not named at all; if you do have to name it, use „von“ + Dativ for a person and „durch“ + Akkusativ for a means or a cause.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Nesne alan hemen her: Almost every verb that takes an object: haben, kaufen, trinken, essen, sehen, suchen, brauchen, möchten. The pattern „Es gibt“ always takes the Akkusativ too.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Fark varsa „als“ kul: For a difference you use „als“, for equality „so … wie“. The commonest slip is „größer wie“; the right form is „größer als“, and English "than" is a safe guide.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Soru kelimesi başa g: The question word comes first, the finite verb stands right behind it in SECOND position, and the subject comes third. A separated prefix still stays at the end of the sentence.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Ortaç değişmez; zama: The participle never changes; it is the auxiliary that carries the tense. In the Präsens it is „wird“, in the Präteritum „wurde“, in the Perfekt „ist … worden“ — not „geworden“.
task.explanation.tr\u0000„Ich habe ein Hund“: „Ich habe ein Hund“ is wrong: Hund is masculine, so it has to be einen Hund. You cannot build an Akkusativ without knowing the article; always learn a noun with its article.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Kökü -t ya da -d ile: Verbs whose stem ends in -t or -d slip in an e for the sake of pronunciation: du arbeitest, er arbeitet. „nehmen“ shortens its stem as well: du nimmst, er nimmt.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Sona giden şey ÇEKİM: What goes to the end is the FINITE verb. With a modal, the infinitive sits second from last and the modal goes right to the end. A separable verb joins up again in a subordinate clause.
task.explanation.tr\u0000İki fiil de üçüncü t: Neither verb TAKES AN ENDING in the third person singular: er war, er hatte. The run is: war, warst, war, waren, wart, waren; hatte, hattest, hatte, hatten, hattet, hatten.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Akkusativ'de kural a: In the Akkusativ the rule is the same as with the article: only the masculine takes -en. mein → meinen, dein → deinen, unser → unseren. The feminine, neuter and plural forms stay as they are.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Cümlede bir modal fi: If the clause has a modal verb, no Partizip II is used; two infinitives line up at the end instead. „Wir hätten das bemerken können“ is right, „gekonnt“ is wrong.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Olmayan bir durumu a: When you describe something that is not the case, BOTH halves need the Konjunktiv II. In the subordinate clause the verb goes last; the main clause is built with „würde“ or with the verb's own form.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Yan cümle önce gelir: If the subordinate clause comes first, the whole of it counts as the first element: the main verb follows straight after the comma and the subject drops in behind it. In short: verb, comma, verb.
task.explanation.tr\u0000İlgi zamiri cinsini: The relative pronoun takes its gender and its number from the noun it DESCRIBES, but its case from the job it does inside the clause. Subject gives der, object den, and a dative role dem.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Nesneyi, bir Partizi: Moving the object, a Partizip or a whole subordinate clause into the Vorfeld puts it in the spotlight. English does the same by fronting ("That I did not expect"), and in writing it sets the tone.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Edat ve artikel çoğu: Preposition and article often merge. In the Dativ, in dem = im and an dem = am; in the Akkusativ, in das = ins and an das = ans. These short forms also give away which case you are in.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Yan cümlede bir edat: If the clause needs a preposition, it comes BEFORE the relative pronoun and it decides the case. English "the city I live in" becomes „die Stadt, in der ich lebe“ — German never strands it at the end.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Bazı fiillerde kökte: In some verbs the stem vowel changes ONLY in the du and er/sie/es forms: a → ä (fahren, schlafen), e → i/ie (sprechen, nehmen, lesen, sehen). With the other persons the stem stays as it is.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Eylemi yapan gerçekt: If the doer really has to be named, people and institutions come with „von“, means and causes with „durch“. In a passive with a modal the order is fixed: Partizip II + werden + the finite modal.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Nesne bir KİŞİ ise d: If the object is a PERSON, no da-/wo- compound is used: „auf ihn“, „mit ihr“, „an wen“. A da- compound can also announce a „dass“ clause or an infinitive that is still to come.
task.explanation.tr\u0000„können“ yetenek ve: „können“ is ability and possibility, „müssen“ obligation, „möchten“ a polite wish. When you say you want to buy something, „ich möchte“ is far more polite than „ich will“.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Çoğulda cins kaybolu: In the plural gender disappears: whatever the singular was, the plural article is always die. And „ein“ has no plural — you either drop the article or, in the negative, use „keine“.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Bu biçim iki anlamı: The form carries both meanings and the context tells you which one. With an adverb of ease („leicht“, „kaum“) it reads as possibility; with an official date or condition, as obligation.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Modal fiiller Präter: In the Präteritum the modals lose the umlaut on their vowel and are conjugated like hatte: können → konnte, müssen → musste, dürfen → durfte, wollen → wollte, sollen → sollte, mögen → mochte.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede fiilin başı: English already does this with phrasal verbs: you turn the light off, not you turn off it. German goes further — some prefixes leave the verb and travel TO THE VERY END. „aufstehen“ is one word in the dictionary and two in a sentence.
Look at the verb. Verbs of position take the Dativ: liegen, stehen, sitzen, hängen, sein, bleiben. Verbs of movement take the Akkusativ: legen, stellen, setzen, hängen, gehen, fahren, kommen.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Beş sıfat kuralın dı: Five adjectives fall outside the rule and turn up constantly: gut → besser → am besten, viel → mehr → am meisten, gern → lieber → am liebsten, hoch → höher → am höchsten, nah → näher → am nächsten.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede „daha büyük: English already puts the ending on short adjectives: big → bigger → biggest. German does the same: groß → größer → am größten. On top of that most short adjectives take an umlaut: alt → älter, jung → jünger, lang → länger.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Hareket bildiren ve: With a verb of motion that takes „sein“, the Partizip II is not passive but COMPLETED and active: „der angekommene Zug“ says the train has arrived, not that somebody brought it in.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Nesne bir NESNE ise: If the object is a THING, you do not say „auf es“; the preposition merges with „da-“: darauf, darüber, daran, damit, davon. In a question „worauf“ replaces „auf was“. If the preposition starts with a vowel, an -r- slips in between.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Partizip I için mast: For the Partizip I you add -d to the infinitive: warten → wartend, passen → passend. The Partizip II is the verb's third form: decken → gedeckt, schreiben → geschrieben. Both then take the ordinary adjective endings.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede kişi ekini: English marks the person once, with the -s of he works. German marks all six, and the ending sits in the same place, at the end of the verb: ich -e, du -st, er/sie/es -t, wir -en, ihr -t, sie/Sie -en.
task.explanation.tr\u0000„werden“ tek başına: On its own „werden“ means to become (Er wird Arzt) and it also builds the future; to see that a sentence is passive, look for the Partizip II at the end. And „sein + Partizip II“ describes the result, not the process.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede tarif ismin: English puts the description AFTER the noun too: the flat I am looking for. German does the same, but with a full clause that starts with der, die or das, and because it is a subordinate clause the finite verb goes to the end.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede mastar eki: English uses a separate word as well: to come, to work. German puts „zu“ in front of the infinitive in the same way, but the phrase stands at the end of the sentence. With separable verbs the „zu“ slips into the middle: anzufangen, mitzukommen.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede ricayı yumu: English softens a request by changing the verb too: can you help becomes could you help. German does exactly that: können → könnten, haben → hätte, sein → wäre.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Vurgulu ön ekler ayr: Stressed prefixes separate: auf-, an-, ab-, aus-, ein-, mit-, zu-, vor-, fern-. Unstressed ones never do: be-, ver-, er-, ent-, ge-. As a rule of thumb, if the stress falls on the prefix when you say the word, it separates.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede tek bir edi: English has the same ambiguity: the shop was closed can mean the act or the state. German splits the two. „werden + Partizip II“ describes the ACT (Vorgangspassiv), „sein + Partizip II“ the STATE (Zustandspassiv).
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede isimlerin c: English nouns have no gender either; in German every noun has an article and it is learnt together with the word. Some endings give the gender away: words in -ung, -heit and -keit are always die, and words in -chen are always das.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Orantı iki karşılaşt: The proportion is built with two comparatives. The half that starts with „je“ is a SUBORDINATE clause, so its verb goes last; the half that starts with „desto“ is the main clause, and its verb comes straight after the „desto + adjective“ phrase.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Bir sıfat cümlesi („: A relative clause („die Studie, die im Mai veröffentlicht wurde“) can be compressed and set BETWEEN the article and the noun. The Partizip I carries an active, ongoing action, the Partizip II a finished or passive one.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede geçmiş tek: English also uses two parts: I have worked. In German the two stand at opposite ends of the sentence: the auxiliary in second position, the participle of the main verb right at the end. Everything else is packed in between.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede tek bir geç: English chooses between I worked and I have worked by meaning; German chooses by verb. In speech most verbs take the Perfekt, but sein, haben and the modals nearly always come in the Präteritum: „Ich war müde“, not „Ich bin müde gewesen“.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede nesneye -i: English marks the object only on the pronoun: he → him, she → her. German marks it on the article instead, and only on the masculine (der) word: der → den, ein → einen. Nothing changes on a feminine (die) or a neuter (das) word.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede yan cümle e: In English a subordinate clause keeps the ordinary order: because I had no time. German starts the same way, verb second in the main clause, but the moment a conjunction appears the finite verb moves to the very end. The comma is compulsory.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Konjunktiv I kökten: The Konjunktiv I is built on the stem and takes the endings -e, -est, -e, -en, -et, -en. Where it really differs from the indicative is the third person singular: er kommt → er komme. „sein“ is irregular: ich sei, du seist, er sei, wir seien.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Birincisi: „obwohl“: First: „obwohl“ and „trotzdem“ are not used together in one sentence; both mark the contrast and one is enough. Second: in the „je … desto“ pattern both halves need a comparative — „je klarer“, not „je klar“.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede „gelseydi,: English uses two different shapes as well: if he had come, we would have seen. German has ONE single form for the past Konjunktiv II: hätte or wäre + Partizip II. Which auxiliary you need is decided by the verb's Perfekt.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede edilgen fii: English needs two words too: it is being sent. German needs the same two, but pulled apart: „werden“ is conjugated in second position and the Partizip II goes to the end. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive one.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Çoğu fiil için günlü: In everyday speech most verbs use „würde + Infinitiv“. But sein, haben and the modals are said in their own short forms: wäre, hätte, könnte, müsste, dürfte, sollte. Using „würde“ with those sounds wrong.
task.explanation.tr\u0000„doch“ beklenenin te: „doch“ contradicts what was expected or softens an order. „ja“ points to something the listener already knows; in an exclamation it signals surprise. „mal“ makes a request casual. „eben“ and „halt“ signal acceptance: that is how it is.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede yetenek ve: English also uses two separate words: I can come, I have to go. In German the two move to opposite ends of the sentence: the modal is conjugated in second position and the main verb stays bare, right at the end.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede duyduğunu a: English shifts the tense when it reports: he says he is coming, he said he was coming. German changes the verb into a different form instead: er sagt, er sei / er habe / er komme. The form carries neither agreement nor denial, it only says: these are his words.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Gerçekdışı benzetmed: An unreal comparison has two structures. „als ob“ opens a subordinate clause and throws the verb to the END. „als“ on its own is followed IMMEDIATELY by the verb. Both need the Konjunktiv; Konjunktiv I and II are both accepted.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Nominal üslup yoğunl: The nominal style condenses, but it tires the reader and makes it easy to hide the agent. The quickest way to make a text clear is to turn nominalised actions back into verbs: „durchführen“ rather than „zur Durchführung bringen“.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Fiillerin çoğu haben: Most verbs take haben. Those that describe going from one place to another (gehen, fahren, kommen, fliegen) and a change of state (aufstehen, einschlafen, werden) take sein. „bleiben“ and „sein“ also go with sein — not a rule, something to learn by heart.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Tekil biçimlerde kök: In the singular the stem vowel changes and the third person TAKES NO -t: ich kann, du kannst, er kann. The same goes for müssen: ich muss, du musst, er muss. „möchten“, on the other hand, is conjugated as if it were regular: ich möchte, du möchtest, er möchte.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Bu parçacıklar cümle: These particles cannot be the first element of a sentence and they never carry stress; stress them and the meaning changes completely („Komm ja mit!“ is a threat). They are also out of place in formal letters, contracts and reports: there you want content, not attitude.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede vurgulanan: In English the subject stands in front of the verb almost without exception. In a German main clause the finite verb is in second position and exactly ONE element stands in front of it. That slot is the Vorfeld; a subject, an object, a time, a place or even a whole subordinate clause can go there.
task.explanation.tr\u0000„ein“, „kein“ ve iye: After „ein“, „kein“ and the possessives the adjective itself shows the gender that the article leaves out: ein kleiner Tisch, eine kleine Lampe, ein kleines Haus. „der/die/das“ already shows the gender, so the adjective stays plain: der kleine Tisch.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede iyelik isme: English also uses a separate word, my, and it never changes. The German word does change, and it looks not at the OWNER but at the gender of the thing owned: mein Bruder (masculine), meine Schwester (feminine), mein Kind (neuter), meine Eltern (plural).
task.explanation.tr\u0000Vorfeld genellikle ö: The Vorfeld usually carries what links back to the previous sentence, that is, KNOWN information; the real news comes towards the end. That is why a sentence like „Daraus folgen zwei Regeln“ reads smoothly: „daraus“ points backwards and „zwei Regeln“ is the new part.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede tek bir ek: English has essentially one ending, -s, with a handful of exceptions. German has five ways: -e (der Tag → die Tage), -er (das Kind → die Kinder), -(e)n (die Frau → die Frauen), -s (das Auto → die Autos) and no ending at all (der Lehrer → die Lehrer). Some of them add an umlaut too.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede „yapılabili: English says it with can be done. German has three lighter forms to set against „kann gemacht werden“: „lässt sich machen“, „ist zu machen“ and „ist machbar“. None of them names the agent, and in formal writing they read more smoothly than the werden passive.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede zıtlığı „-m: English builds the contrast with although, nevertheless or despite. In German the word you pick decides the order: „obwohl“ opens a subordinate clause and throws the verb to the end, „trotzdem“ is an element in a main clause, and „trotz“ is a preposition that takes the Genitiv.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Çoğu fiilde ge- + kö: For most verbs it is ge- + stem + -t: kaufen → gekauft. Strong verbs end in -en and can change their vowel: sehen → gesehen. With separable verbs the ge- moves into the middle: einkaufen → eingekauft. Verbs in -ieren and verbs beginning with be-, ver- or er- TAKE NO ge-.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Çoğul biçimlerde Kon: In the plural the Konjunktiv I looks exactly like the indicative (wir kommen). So that the report does not become unreadable, you switch to the Konjunktiv II: sie kämen, sie hätten, sie begännen. For the past there is one single form: er habe … gesehen, sie sei … gekommen.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede iki ayrı or: English has two participles as well: the waiting guests (the one doing it) and the laid table (the one it was done to). German has the same pair: the Partizip I for an ongoing action, the Partizip II for a completed one. Both stand in front of the noun and take adjective endings.
task.explanation.tr\u0000„-bar“ eki yalnız ne: The „-bar“ suffix is only formed from verbs that take an object: messbar, lesbar, vermeidbar, machbar. It is not derived from verbs like „gehen“ or „schlafen“. Some forms are well established, others sound invented; if you are not sure, „lässt sich“ is always safe.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Fiil cümlesi olayı z: A verbal clause tells you the event with its time and its agent; a noun phrase compresses the same event and can hide both. English does the same with heavy noun phrases, but in German it is a style decision: institutional writing goes nominal, speech and good journalism go verbal.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede fark ekte g: In English the difference shows in the preposition itself: on the table, onto the table. In German the preposition stays the same (auf) and the article changes: auf dem Tisch (Dativ, place) ↔ auf den Tisch (Akkusativ, direction). Nine prepositions work this way: in, an, auf, unter, über, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede bu işi tonl: English does this job with intonation and with words like "you know", "just", "after all" and an emphatic "do". German has four little particles that carry the same load: doch, ja, mal, eben. They do not change the information in the sentence, they carry the speaker's attitude; they are unstressed and they sit in the middle of the clause.
task.explanation.tr\u0000Türkçede nesnenin hâ: English fixes a preposition to many verbs too: wait for, think about, ask for. German does the same but picks different ones, and the preposition is learnt together with the verb: warten auf, denken an, sich freuen über, bitten um, sich kümmern um, rechnen mit, achten auf.

task.monologue.promptTr\u0000Dürüstlük ne zam: When is honesty a gift and when is it a burden? Build a criterion that goes beyond the easy answer "always be honest" and test it with examples.
task.monologue.promptTr\u0000Bazı işler evden: Some jobs can be done from home as well. Do you think people should work from home or at the workplace? Give your opinion and at least two reasons.
task.monologue.promptTr\u0000Komşularını tanı: Is it necessary to know your neighbours? Give your opinion, give at least two reasons, one practical and one human, and leave room for the opposing view.
task.monologue.promptTr\u0000Üçüncü bir yaban: Is it worth learning a third foreign language? Give your opinion, give an example from your own experience and say in which case it would not be worth it.
task.monologue.promptTr\u0000İyi bir eğitimi: How do you recognise good training (vocational training, a course, an apprenticeship)? Test the common criterion, break your own criterion into at least two parts and make each part concrete.
task.monologue.promptTr\u0000Bir kurumda neyi: Separate what can be settled by rules in an organisation from what cannot. Test your distinction with an example and say what you would suggest for the part that cannot.
task.monologue.promptTr\u0000Bir toplulukta d: Is order in a community achieved through detailed rules or through trust? Compare the two approaches, show the weak side of each and state your own criterion.
task.monologue.promptTr\u0000Bazı şirketler h: Some companies are trying a four-day week: same pay, same work, one day less. Weigh the model up: who does it work for, who does it not work for, what do you think?
task.monologue.promptTr\u0000Yaşadığın yerde: If you could change one single thing where you live, what would it be? Say what you would choose, explain why it matters and give a concrete idea of how it could be done.
task.monologue.promptTr\u0000Bazı sokaklar ta: Some streets carry the names of controversial figures. Should such names be changed, or is an explanatory plaque enough? Weigh up both sides, then state your own position.
task.monologue.promptTr\u0000Bir aksaklıktan: After something goes wrong people often say "this could have been foreseen". When is that judgement fair and when is it not? Take a position, do justice to the other side and set out your own criterion.
task.monologue.promptTr\u0000Küçük işletmeler: Should accessibility be compulsory for small businesses, or should it be left voluntary with incentives? Compare the two approaches, show a weak point in each and state your own criterion.
task.monologue.promptTr\u0000Bazıları özel gü: Some people think presents matter on special occasions, others say time spent together is worth more. What do you think? State your preference and support it with at least two reasons.
task.monologue.promptTr\u0000Çeviri araçları: Translation tools now give understandable results in most situations. Does that make learning a foreign language unnecessary? Defend your position, present the strongest counter-argument as well and say where you draw the line.
task.monologue.promptTr\u0000Kurumların ürett: Should the texts organisations produce — guidelines, forms, information sheets — be tested with people who do not know them before they are published? Take a position, present the strongest objection and set out your own criterion.
task.monologue.rubricHint\u0000İki yaklaşımın: The strong and the weak side of both approaches has to come up; „obwohl“, „trotzdem“ and „je … desto“ are expected.
task.monologue.rubricHint\u0000Konum, karşı a: Position, counter-argument and condition must all be there; the register (Register) has to be consistent and abstract at C1 level.
task.monologue.rubricHint\u0000Edilgen yerine: Structures that stand in for the passive are expected (lässt sich, ist zu …, -bar) and the distinction has to be tested with a concrete example.
task.monologue.rubricHint\u0000Konjunktiv II: The Konjunktiv II is expected (würde, wäre, könnte); the suggestion has to be concrete and at least one opposing view has to be accepted.
task.monologue.rubricHint\u0000Ölçüt en az üç: The criterion has to be broken into at least three parts and each part tested with an example; modal particles should appear naturally.
task.monologue.rubricHint\u0000Konjunktiv II: The past form of the Konjunktiv II is expected (hätte prüfen müssen, wäre gewesen) and the criterion has to be broken into at least two parts.
task.monologue.rubricHint\u0000Her iki taraf: Both sides have to appear with their reasons and the conclusion has to be tied to a condition; nominal and passive structures are expected at B2.
task.monologue.rubricHint\u0000Yaygın ölçüt s: The common criterion has to be tested and the speaker's own criterion broken into at least two parts; verbs with prepositions and da-/wo- compounds are expected.
task.monologue.rubricHint\u0000İki tarafın da: The strongest argument on each side has to come up and the conclusion has to be differentiated (not the same answer in every case); connectives are expected.
task.monologue.rubricHint\u0000Görüş gerekçes: The opinion has to come with its reason and at least one counter-argument has to be there; in „weil“ and „dass“ clauses the verb has to be at the end.
task.monologue.rubricHint\u0000Kendi deneyimi: A concrete example from the speaker's own experience is expected and a limitation has to be stated; „um … zu“ and „statt … zu“ can be used.
task.monologue.rubricHint\u0000Tercih tek cüm: The preference has to be clear in a single sentence, with at least two reasons and one counter-example; in „wenn“ and „dass“ clauses the verb has to be at the end.
task.monologue.rubricHint\u0000Soru yeniden ç: The question has to be reframed, the strongest objection accepted and the criterion tested with examples from both extremes; the Vorfeld choices have to be deliberate.
task.monologue.rubricHint\u0000İki farklı tür: Two different kinds of reason are expected (practical and human) and the opposing view has to be accepted; in „wenn“ and „dass“ clauses the verb has to be at the end.
task.monologue.rubricHint\u0000İki yaklaşımın: The strong and the weak side of both approaches has to come up; the conclusion has to be differentiated by a single criterion, and a flat answer like "make it all compulsory" is not enough.

task.monologue.bulletsTr\u0000Sorunun neden „: Say why the question does not end with "always be honest"
task.monologue.bulletsTr\u0000En az iki gerek: Give at least two reasons (time, money, contact, family…)
task.monologue.bulletsTr\u0000İşlemediği bir: Describe a case where it does not work (shift work, care, service)
task.monologue.bulletsTr\u0000Kendi konumunu: Finish by differentiating your position (what in which case)
task.monologue.bulletsTr\u0000Kimin itiraz ed: Say who would object and why they are right
task.monologue.bulletsTr\u0000İkinci ölçütünü: Give your second criterion: in what order responsibility is handed over
task.monologue.bulletsTr\u0000Yaygın ölçütü a: Name the common criterion and say why it is not enough
task.monologue.bulletsTr\u0000Yargının neden: Show why the judgement is both true and useless
task.monologue.bulletsTr\u0000Yargıyı tümden: Say why rejecting the judgement outright is the easy way out
task.monologue.bulletsTr\u0000Alışıldık „daha: Set aside the usual question of "more rules or fewer"
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Buna güvenmezd: I would not rely on that.
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Bu ilk adım ol: That would be a first step.
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Üç kez söyleni: If you name them three times, …
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Vakit varsa …: If there is time, I would …
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000İlk ölçütüm …: My first criterion has to do with …
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Ölçütüm … deği: My criterion would not be …, but …
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Bana belirleyi: What seems decisive to me is …
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Ancak dürüst o: One has to be honest, though: …
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000… olarak ele a: It is treated as …; in fact it is …
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Bir şeyi değiş: If I could change one thing, …
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Değer, ama … o: It is worth it, but not because …
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Yine de … fazl: Even so, it would be too easy to …
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Elbette bazıla: Of course some people would object.
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000İlk ölçütüm ta: That is exactly what my first criterion would be: …
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Bu yüzden … ol: That is why I think that …
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Buna karşı güç: There is a strong objection to that.
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Bunun başka tü: That has to be handled differently.
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Ne hakkında ko: I would pay attention to what is being talked about
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Bu bakımdan bu: In that sense it only holds on condition that …
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Gönüllülük yal: Voluntary action only reaches those who already …
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Dürüstlük zate: Honesty is not a property of the statement.
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Peşinen: Soruy: To start with: I think the question is wrongly put, because …
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000İnsanın değerl: You simply have to say what you cannot judge.
task.monologue.targets.tr\u0000Neredeyse hiç: It is almost never tested, and there is a reason for that.

task.drill.hint\u0000İki kez şt: ştu-DİİRT ve: Two lots of sht: shtoo-DEERT and SHTUT-gart.
task.drill.hint\u0000„meine“ = MAY-ne; „liebt: „meine“ = MY-nuh; „liebt“ = LEEPT, with a long i.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Tür“ uzun ü, „zu“ uzun: „Tür“ has a long ü, „zu“ a long u. „mach“ has a short a.
task.drill.hint\u0000„schreibe“ = ŞRAY-be; „B: „schreibe“ = SHRY-buh; „Brief“ = BREEF, with a long i.
task.drill.hint\u0000„spielen“ = ŞPİİ-len: ba: „spielen“ = SHPEE-len: sp at the start is shp, ie is a long i.
task.drill.hint\u0000Burada st kelimenin SONU: Here st is at the END of the word: BIST, and not sht this time.
task.drill.hint\u0000Üç kez ts: „zum“, „Zahn-: Three lots of ts: „zum“, „Zahn-“ and the z at the end of „-arzt“.
task.drill.hint\u0000„gehen“ uzun e, „jetzt“: „gehen“ has a long e, „jetzt“ a short e, „schlafen“ a long a.
task.drill.hint\u0000„nehmen“ içindeki h duyu: The h inside „nehmen“ is not heard: NAY-men, with a long e.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Oma“ uzun o (OO-ma), „k: „Oma“ has a long o (OH-ma), „kommt“ and „Sonntag“ a short o.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Wagen“ = VAA-gen; „von“: „Wagen“ = VAA-gen; „von“ and „Viktor“ both start with an f.
task.drill.hint\u0000Burada st kelimenin ORTA: Here st is in the MIDDLE of the word: FENS-ter, and not sht.
task.drill.hint\u0000„mein“ ve „heißt“: ay. „: „mein“ and „heißt“: like the y in my. „Dieter“: a long ee — DEE-ter.
task.drill.hint\u0000„wir“ ve „warten“ v ile,: „wir“ and „warten“ take a v, „vor“ an f: foa dem Kino.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Miete“ = Mİİ-te, uzun i: „Miete“ = MEE-tuh, with a long i. „billig“ ends in a soft -ich.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Restaurant“ sonda vurgu: „Restaurant“ is stressed at the end, „Marktplatz“ at the beginning.
task.drill.hint\u0000„zuerst“ = tsu-ERST, iki: „zuerst“ = tsu-ERST, two syllables with the stress on the second one.
task.drill.hint\u0000„heute“ = HOY-te, „neunt: „heute“ = HOY-tuh, „neunte“ = NOY-tuh. „eu“ is always read as oy.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Küche“ ve „nicht“: ince: „Küche“ and „nicht“: the soft ch, because ü and i come before it.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Männer“ kısa e, „spät“: „Männer“ has a short e, „spät“ a long e. Neither has the y sound of my.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Mittwoch“: kalın ch. „i: „Mittwoch“: the hard ch. „ich“: the soft ch. Both in the same sentence.
task.drill.hint\u0000„wie“ ve „viel“ uzun i;: „wie“ and „viel“ have a long i; „Eis“ = EYES, and the final s must be heard.
task.drill.hint\u0000„wie“ ve „Wasser“ v sesi: „wie“ and „Wasser“ have a v sound, „viel“ an f sound: FEEL, not VEEL.
task.drill.hint\u0000„be-“ ayrılmayan ön ekti: „be-“ is an inseparable prefix and it never takes the stress: be-TSAA-len.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Kinder“ ve „hinter“ son: The -er at the end of „Kinder“ and „hinter“ is the same: KIN-da, HIN-ta.
task.drill.hint\u0000Tek başına „ä“ Türkçedek: „ä“ on its own is the e of bed: ER-gert, fer-SHPAY-tung.
task.drill.hint\u0000„mache“: kalın ch. „ich“: „mache“: the hard ch. „ich“ and „nicht“: the soft ch. Three in one sentence.
task.drill.hint\u0000Dört kez kelime başında: Four word-initial h sounds — the sentence is a breathing exercise in itself.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Zimmer“ = TSİ-mer, „zu“: „Zimmer“ = TSI-mer, „zu“ = TSOO. Both words open with the same ts sound.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Straße“ = ŞTRAA-se, „st: „Straße“ = SHTRAA-suh, „still“ = SHTIL. st at the start of a word is sht.
task.drill.hint\u0000Birleşik kelimede ilk pa: In a compound the first part takes the stress: BAAN-hof, KRAN-ken-house.
task.drill.hint\u0000„freue“ = FROY-e; sondak: „freue“ = FROY-uh; the final e is a light syllable of its own at the end.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Freundin“ ve „neue“ eu: „Freundin“ and „neue“ have eu, „Bäume“ äu — all three are the same oy.
task.drill.hint\u0000„tz“ de ts okunur: Zİ-ts: „tz“ is also ts: TSI-tsen. „zusammen“ = tsu-ZA-men, stressed in the middle.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Wann“ = VAN, „von“ = FO: „Wann“ = VAN, „von“ = FON. They follow each other, so they get mixed up.
task.drill.hint\u0000Birleşik kelimede ikinci: In a compound the second part behaves like a new word: Halte-SHTE-luh.
task.drill.hint\u0000Ön ek sayılmaz: „ver-ste: The prefix does not count: „ver-stehe“ has st on the stem, so fer-SHTAY-uh.
task.drill.hint\u0000„wohin“ iki hecelidir ve: „wohin“ has two syllables and the h opens the second: vo-HIN, breathed out.
task.drill.hint\u0000„zehn“ = TSEEN. Önce t,: „zehn“ = TSAYN. First the t, then the s; say it fast, as a single sound.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Häuser“ = HOY-za, „teue: „Häuser“ = HOY-za, „teuer“ = TOY-a. The final -er is weak again, like an a.
task.drill.hint\u0000„spielen“ = ŞPİİ-len, „S: „spielen“ = SHPEE-len, „Sportplatz“ = SHPORT-plats. sp at the start is shp.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Tochter“ ve „kocht“: ik: „Tochter“ and „kocht“: the hard ch in both, because an „o“ comes before it.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Vater“ = FAA-ter, „vier: „Vater“ = FAA-ter, „vier“ = FEER. This v is an f, and it carries no voice.
task.drill.hint\u0000Üç kez kelime başında h:: Three word-initial h sounds: HUNT, HAT, HEEA. A small breath in each of them.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Bruder“ içinde iki fark: Two different r sounds in „Bruder“: BROO-da — the first from the throat, the last an a.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Sommer“ kısa o, „See“ u: „Sommer“ has a short o, „See“ a long e. Two vowels together lengthen the sound.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Zug“ = TSUUK, „zwölf“ =: „Zug“ = TSOOK, „zwölf“ = TSVÖLF — the w that follows a z is read as a v.
task.drill.hint\u0000Baştaki r boğazdan, garg: The initial r comes from the throat, as if gargling. It is not the English r.
task.drill.hint\u0000Emir cümlesinde de ayrıl: In an imperative the separated prefix still stands last and stressed: … früher AUF.
task.drill.hint\u0000Üç kelimede de h kelime: All three words start with h: breathe out lightly, as if blowing out a candle.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Buch“: kalın ch. Ses bo: „Buch“: the hard ch. The sound comes from the back, carrying the „u“ onwards.
task.drill.hint\u0000„ihn“ uzun i (İİN), „in“: „ihn“ has a long i (EEN), „in“ a short one. The h is not heard, it only lengthens.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Zucker“ = TSU-ker, orta: „Zucker“ = TSU-ker, the ck in the middle is a hard k. The final -er sounds like a.
task.drill.hint\u0000Ayrılabilen ön ek vurguy: The separable prefix carries the stress: the „AN“ at the end is said strongly.
task.drill.hint\u0000„besuchen“: kalın ch. „S: „besuchen“: the hard ch. The „sch“ that opens „Schwester“ is a single sh sound.
task.drill.hint\u0000Aynı cümlede iki ses: „L: Two sounds in one sentence: „Läufst“ is oy, „Bäcker“ is e. Alike in writing, not in sound.
task.drill.hint\u0000„be-suchen“ vurgusuz ön: „be-suchen“ has an unstressed prefix, „GROSS-eltern“ is a compound: first part stressed.
task.drill.hint\u0000Üç kelimede de w: VİR VO: All three words take a w: VEER VOO-nen … VALT-shtraa-suh. Lower lip on the upper teeth.
task.drill.hint\u0000„wohne“ uzun o (VOO-ne),: „wohne“ has a long o (VOO-nuh), „Stadt“ a short a (SHTAT). The final dt is one t.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Ofen“ uzun o (OO-fen),: „Ofen“ has a long o (OH-fen), „offen“ a short one. A double consonant means a short vowel.
task.drill.hint\u0000Üç kez zayıf r: Schwesta: Three weak r sounds: Schwesta, Somma, tsu-RÜK — and the last one has a real throat r.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Herr“ ve „Krause“ boğaz: „Herr“ and „Krause“ need the throat r; at the end of „fährt“ the r turns into a: FEEAT.
task.drill.hint\u0000Yabancı kökenli kelimele: In words of foreign origin the stress usually moves back: shtoo-DEERT, in-for-MAA-tik.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Ihr“, „Sohn“ ve „sehr“: The h in „Ihr“, „Sohn“ and „sehr“ is silent; only the h opening „höflich“ is said.
task.drill.hint\u0000„gehe“ ve „zehn“ içindek: The h in „gehe“ and „zehn“ is not heard, it lengthens the vowel. The h in „Hause“ is said.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Regen“ başta boğaz r'si: „Regen“ opens with the throat r; at the end of „Der“ and „hört“ the r weakens to a: dea, höat.
task.drill.hint\u0000İstisna: yabancı kökenli: An exception: in words of foreign origin „v“ is still a v — VAA-ze. „Fenster“ has a real f.
task.drill.hint\u0000„Wasser“ sonu „a“; „wirk: „Wasser“ ends in a; „wirklich“ and „sehr“ differ: a weak r inside the syllable against an a at the end.
task.drill.hint\u0000„ich“ ve „möchte“: ince: „ich“ and „möchte“: the soft ch. The middle of the tongue rises and the air hisses through — not sh, and never k.
task.drill.fix\u0000„äu“ oy, tek „ä“ e: LOYFS: „äu“ is oy, plain „ä“ is e: LOYFST but BE-ka.
task.drill.fix\u0000Kelime sonundaki st norma: At the end of a word st stays ordinary: bist.
task.drill.fix\u0000„o“dan sonra ch boğazdan: After an „o“ the ch comes from the throat, not a k.
task.drill.fix\u0000„W“ hep v, „V“ hep f: VAA: „W“ is always v, „V“ always f: VAA-gen fon FIK-tor.
task.drill.fix\u0000Baştaki st'yi s ile söyle: Do not say the initial st with a plain s: shtraa-suh, shtil.
task.drill.fix\u0000İlk iki kelime v, üçüncüs: The first two words take a v, the third an f. „vor“ = foor.
task.drill.fix\u0000Ortadaki st şt olmaz; nor: st in the middle does not become sht; plain s + t: fenster.
task.drill.fix\u0000„Buch“ sonunu „k“ yapma;: Do not end „Buch“ with a k; carry the sound on in the throat.
task.drill.fix\u0000„ei“ = ay: blay-be. „blie: „ei“ = y: bly-buh. „bliebe“ is a different form altogether.
task.drill.fix\u0000„eu“ oy, arkasından gelen: „eu“ is oy, and the e that follows is not swallowed: fro-yuh.
task.drill.fix\u0000„ü“den sonra ch incedir;: After „ü“ the ch is soft; do not slide it towards an sh.
task.drill.fix\u0000„Eis“ sonundaki s'yi söyl: Say the s at the end of „Eis“; „Ei“ on its own means egg.
task.drill.fix\u0000„u“dan sonra ch boğazdan;: After „u“ the ch comes from the throat; do not confuse it with „sch“.
task.drill.fix\u0000Baştaki ts'yi söyle ve ik: Say the ts at the start and keep the two syllables apart: tsu-erst.
task.drill.fix\u0000„ä“ ay değil e sesidir; a: „ä“ is not y but e; for the y sound German writes „ei“.
task.drill.fix\u0000„ie“ uzun i: şpiilen. Fii: „ie“ is a long i: shpeelen. The verb is plural: it has to end in -en.
task.drill.fix\u0000„Vase“ yabancı kelime, bu: „Vase“ is a foreign word, so v and not f: vaa-zuh.
task.drill.fix\u0000Kelime başındaki sp şp ok: sp at the start of a word is read shp: shpeelen, shportplats.
task.drill.fix\u0000Tek m'li „Oma“ uzun, çift: „Oma“ with one m is long, „kommt“ with two is short.
task.drill.fix\u0000Baştaki ses ts; İngilizce: The first sound is ts; do not read it like the English „sugar“: tsu-ka.
task.drill.fix\u0000„Haus“ çoğul olunca äu al: The plural of „Haus“ takes äu and the sound turns to oy: hoy-za.
task.drill.fix\u0000İkinci parçayı yükseltme;: Do not lift the second part; the first one dominates: BAAN-hof.
task.drill.fix\u0000„ei“ = ay: şray-be. Uzun: „ei“ = y: shry-buh. Said with a long i it becomes another verb.
task.drill.fix\u0000„Zug“ ve „zwölf“ ts ile b: „Zug“ and „zwölf“ open with ts; „zw“ is ts + v: tsvölf.
task.drill.fix\u0000Ön eki yutar gibi hafif s: Say the prefix lightly, almost swallowed, the stress is on the stem: be-tsaa-len.
task.drill.fix\u0000„ie“ uzun i: Miite. Kısa: „ie“ is a long i: Mee-tuh. Said short it turns into „Mitte“ (middle).
task.drill.fix\u0000Baştaki z'yi s gibi söyle: Do not say the initial z like an s; open with ts: tsi-mer, tsoo.
task.drill.fix\u0000Soru kelimesi v ile, edat: The question word takes a v, the preposition an f: VAN … FON DER AR-byt.
task.drill.fix\u0000Vurgu fiil kökünde değil,: The stress is not on the verb stem but on the prefix at the end: … shpay-ta AN.
task.drill.fix\u0000Hem baştaki z hem sondaki: Both the z at the start and the z at the end are ts: tsum TSAAN-artst.
task.drill.fix\u0000„ie“ uzun i: Diiter. Kısa: „ie“ is a long i: Dee-ter. Said short, another name is heard.
task.drill.fix\u0000„ie“ uzun i: liibt. „lebt: „ie“ is a long i: leept. „lebt“ (is alive) is a completely different word.
task.drill.fix\u0000„schlafen“ tek f ile yazı: „schlafen“ is written with one f, so the a is long: SHLAA-fen.
task.drill.fix\u0000Ön ek fiile geri yapışmaz: The prefix does not stick back onto the verb and it keeps the stress: shteh … AUF.
task.drill.fix\u0000Baştaki r boğazdan, sonda: The r at the start is from the throat, the one at the end is a: her but KROW-zuh, fee-at.
task.drill.fix\u0000„a“dan sonra kalın, „i“de: Hard after an „a“, soft after an „i“; do not turn either of them into an sh.
task.drill.fix\u0000„z“ Türkçedeki z değil: d: The German z is not an English z: the tip of the tongue makes t, then s — tsayn.
task.drill.fix\u0000„ich“ sonunu „ş“ ya da „k: Do not end „ich“ with an sh or a k; let it out as a soft breath instead.
task.drill.fix\u0000„Wasser“ = VA-sa, „sehr“: „Wasser“ = VA-sa, „sehr“ = zea. In both of them the final r is swallowed.
task.drill.fix\u0000Aynı cümlede iki farklı s: There are two different sounds in the sentence: „viel“ with f, „Wasser“ with v.
task.drill.fix\u0000Hem fiilde hem şehir adın: st is sht at the start of both the verb and the city name: shtu-deert, shtut-gart.
task.drill.fix\u0000Ortadaki h ne nefes ne de: The h in the middle is neither a breath nor a ch; it only lengthens the e: nay-men.
task.drill.fix\u0000„Sommer“ çift m yüzünden: „Sommer“ is short because of the double m; „See“ is long because of the double e: zay.
task.drill.fix\u0000İki kelimede de son hece: In both words the last syllable is light, like -da and -ta; the r is not heard.
task.drill.fix\u0000Üçünü de üfleyerek söyle;: Breathe all three of them out; drop one and the sentence stops sounding German.
task.drill.fix\u0000Yabancı kelime sonda, Alm: The foreign word is stressed at the end, the German compound at the beginning.
task.drill.fix\u0000Aynı cümlede iki ayrı ch: There are two different ch sounds in one sentence; „Mittwoch“ from the throat, „ich“ from the palate.
task.drill.fix\u0000İki harfi ayrı ayrı söyle: Do not say the two letters separately; they make a single oy: hoy-tuh, noyn-tuh.
task.drill.fix\u0000„w“ ne u ne b: Türkçedeki: „w“ is neither a u nor a b: it is the English v, voiced between lip and teeth.
task.drill.fix\u0000Kısa ya da uzun olabilir: It can be short or long, but „ä“ always belongs to the e family: MEN-na, SHPAYT.
task.drill.fix\u0000Bu iki kelimede vurgu baş: In these two words the stress is not on the first syllable but on the last but one.
task.drill.fix\u0000Ön ekten sonra kök „stehe: After the prefix the stem begins with „stehen“, so it is sht again: fer-shtay-uh.
task.drill.fix\u0000„Stelle“ birleşiğin içind: „Stelle“ starts a new word inside the compound, so sht: halte-shte-luh.
task.drill.fix\u0000„sitzen“ ortasındaki tz t: The tz in the middle of „sitzen“ is one ts sound; „zusammen“ opens with ts.
task.drill.fix\u0000Bir kelimede vurgu kökte,: In one word the stress is on the stem, in the other on the first part: be-ZOO-hen, GROHS-eltern.
task.drill.fix\u0000Sondaki -er hecesini „er“: Do not say the final -er syllable as er, finish it like an a: broo-da, ar-by-tet.
task.drill.fix\u0000Kelime sonundaki r'yi yuv: Do not roll the r at the end of a word: höat, dea. Only „Regen“ has a real r.
task.drill.fix\u0000Baştaki h'yi yutma; ama T: Do not swallow the initial h, but do not make it harsh either — it is only a breath.
task.drill.fix\u0000Burada h ünlüden sonra de: Here the h does not follow a vowel, it opens a new syllable, so it is heard: vo-hin.
task.drill.fix\u0000Dil ucunu titretme; ses k: Do not trill the tip of the tongue; the sound comes from the back, where the uvula sits.
task.drill.fix\u0000Ünlüden sonraki h sessizd: An h after a vowel is silent: gay-uh, tsayn. Only „Hause“ opens with a real breath.
task.drill.fix\u0000-er ile bitenlerde r yok,: Words ending in -er have no r but an a; the r inside „zurück“ does come from the throat.
task.drill.fix\u0000Dört h'nin dördü de üflen: All four h sounds are breathed out; none of them is silent, because all four open a word.
task.drill.fix\u0000Üç kelimede h yalnız uzat: In three words the h only lengthens: eea, zohn, zea. The fourth has a breath: HÖÖF-lich.
task.drill.fix\u0000„Tür“ uzun ü ile; ayrıca: „Tür“ has a long ü; and „zu“ belongs to the verb here, said with ts and a long u.
task.drill.fix\u0000İlki uzun (iin), ikincisi: The first one is long (een), the second short (in); say them alike and the sentence loses its sense.
task.drill.fix\u0000Almancada „v“ genelde f o: In German „v“ is usually read as f: faa-ter, feer. Say it as a v and another word is heard.
task.drill.fix\u0000„wohne“ içindeki h ünlüyü: The h inside „wohne“ lengthens the vowel; „Stadt“ has a short a — said long it becomes „Staat“ (state).
task.drill.fix\u0000Tek sessizden önce ünlü u: A vowel lengthens before a single consonant and shortens before a double one: OH-fen but not O-fen, of-fen.
