task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi bağlayıcı hâ: Make the sentence binding: keep the commitment, drop the escape clause.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi düzelt: kriz: Correct the sentence: rank and authority are muddled in a crisis meeting.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi düzelt: yaza: Correct the sentence: the writer means to guess but signals doubt instead.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Doğrudan talebi Konj: Use the Konjunktiv II to leave the direct demand open to negotiation.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000İltifatı düzelt: sıc: Correct the compliment: the warmth is excessive here and works against you.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi doğru hâlle: Rewrite the sentence with the right case: with this symptom the person is not the subject.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi yargısız hâl: Make the sentence non-judgemental: keep the fact, drop the accusation.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Aracılık cümlesini d: Correct the interpreting: the interpreter has mixed in an opinion of their own.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi düzelt: dola: Correct the sentence: part of the indirect question is built like a main clause.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi düzelt: kısm: Correct the sentence: partial agreement has become full agreement and the distinction is lost.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi devrik kur:: Front the time phrase: the emphasis belongs on the time, not on the subject.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi düzelt: sözc: Correct the sentence: the word chosen carries an accusation that was not meant.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi doğru hâlle: Rewrite the sentence with the right case: the person who feels it is not the subject.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi düzelt: ayrı: Correct the sentence: the past form of the separable verb is built wrongly.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi düzelt: bura: Correct the sentence: two things are being compared, not ranked top.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi referans mek: Turn the sentence into the language of a reference: use a participle and the passive.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi düzelt: yaza: Correct the sentence: the writer presents someone else's accusation as their own claim.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi düzelt: yan: Correct the sentence: the subordinate clause comes first, so the main clause order has to change.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi düzelt: taml: Correct the sentence: the wrong case follows a preposition that takes the Genitiv.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi günlük dile: Turn the sentence into everyday language: with a time adverb, werden is dead weight.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi Alman ölçeği: Bring the sentence down to a German scale: the overstatement produces vagueness, not warmth.
task.rewrite.prompt\u0000Cümleyi düzelt: akta: Correct the sentence: in reporting it, the writer presents someone else's claim as their own.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Resmî hitapta „bist du“: In the formal form „sind Sie“ replaces „bist du“.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„du kommst“ → „Sie komm: „du kommst“ → „Sie kommen“. In the formal form the verb is kommen.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„einfach“ tek yön, „hin: „einfach“ means one way, „hin und zurück“ means a return.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„eine“ olumsuzda „keine: In the negative „eine“ becomes „keine“. For masculine and neuter, „ein“ → „kein“.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Bu bağlaçtan sonra fiil: After this conjunction the verb goes not into second position but RIGHT TO THE END.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Suçlamayı çıkar, isteği: Take out the accusation, put the request into the subjunctive and offer a talk.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Resmî hâlde özne „Sie“: In the formal form the subject is „Sie“ (a capital letter) and the verb ends in „-en“: heißen Sie.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Bu iki fiil konuşmada P: These two verbs do not go into the Perfekt in speech: bin → war, habe → hatte.
task.rewrite.why\u0000ge- kelimenin başına de: The ge- does not go at the front of the word but after the prefix — mit-ge-nommen.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Sıfatı olumsuzlamak içi: To negate an adjective, „nicht“ comes IN FRONT of it: nicht richtig.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Duvardaki resim ASILIDI: A picture on the wall HANGS, it does not stand — so „hängen“ is used.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Kip fiilleri konuşmada: Modal verbs do not form the Perfekt in speech; the simple past is used instead.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„gar nicht“ = hiç. „nic: „gar nicht“ = not at all. It is stronger than „nicht“ and stands at the end.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„lieber“ fiilden sonra: „lieber“ comes after the verb and adds the sense of „I would rather …“.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Yan cümlede çekimli fii: In a subordinate clause the finite verb goes last; the time adverb stays in front of it.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„empfehlen“ doğrudan Ak: „empfehlen“ takes the Akkusativ directly: Ich empfehle die Kirche / das Museum.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„verlieren“ kuralsız: o: „verlieren“ is irregular: its participle is „verloren“ and it takes no „ge“, the prefix being unstressed.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„wie“ benzerlik bildiri: „wie“ marks likeness (so stark wie); a comparison is always built with „als“.
task.rewrite.why\u0000İki nesne de zamir olun: When both objects are pronouns the accusative one comes first: ihn dir, not „dir ihn“.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„Ich will“ kaba durur;: „Ich will“ sounds rude; when you order something you say „Ich möchte“ or „Ich hätte gern“.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Dolaylı soru yan cümled: An indirect question is a subordinate clause: the question order (kann ich) breaks up and the finite verb goes last.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Yabancıya soru sorarken: When you ask a stranger a question, starting with „Entschuldigung“ is all but obligatory in German.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Yönetmelikte kişiye değ: Regulations address everybody rather than one person; so „man“ is used instead of „du“.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„helfen“ kişiyi yönelme: „helfen“ puts the person in the dative, not the accusative. Everybody gets this one wrong.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„nicht so gut“ kibar bi: „nicht so gut“ is a polite negative: saying you are not very good at it without saying you cannot do it at all.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Resmî emirde fiil tam b: In a formal instruction the verb takes its full form and Sie is said; the du form sounds rude in a formal setting.
task.rewrite.why\u0000als yalnız karşılaştırm: als only goes with a comparative; am ...-sten stands on its own and takes no als beside it.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Fiili sona atan „weil“;: It is „weil“ that sends the verb to the end; after „denn“ the sentence is built normally and the verb stays second.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçedeki '-in hâli' A: The English of-phrase becomes the Genitiv in German: not 'von die Kosten' but 'der Kosten'.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„mit“ ve „ohne“ karşıtt: „mit“ and „ohne“ are opposites; „ohne“ takes the Akkusativ, but „Ei“ is neuter so the form does not change.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Öznesi olayın kendisi,: The event is the subject and the person stands in the dative — just as English says „it was very unpleasant for me“.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Reddederken „leider“ il: A refusal opens with „leider“; to avoid sounding rude you add a reason or a new suggestion.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Resmî hitapta özne Sie,: In the formal form the subject is Sie, the verb ends in -en (schreiben Sie), and „Ihren“ replaces „deinen“.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Almanya'da hava sohbeti: Small talk about the weather is a form of politeness in Germany; it is not there to give information but to open a conversation.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Yazıldığı gibi „ben baş: As written it means „I make other people dizzy“. English puts the person in the subject; German puts whoever has the symptom in the dative.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„essen“ yer değiştirme: „essen“ is not a change of place → haben. The participle „gegessen“ goes to the end; „mit Elif“ stays inside the bracket.
task.rewrite.why\u0000mitbringen iki nesne al: mitbringen takes two objects: the thing brought in the accusative, the person it is brought to in the dative — meinem with a masculine noun.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Zaman öne alınınca fiil: When the time phrase is fronted the verb stays in second position and the subject moves behind it; the separable prefix still stands at the end.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Belirsiz artikel ismin: The indefinite article does not show the gender, so the adjective takes that job over and ends in two letters with a neuter noun.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Nokta bildiren „vor“ ge: „vor“ marks a point and goes with the past, „seit“ marks a stretch and goes with the present — and the verb changes along with it.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Renk adı olarak kullanı: Used as the name of a colour it takes a CAPITAL letter: in Blau, in Rot. As an adjective it stays lower case: Der Pullover ist blau.
task.rewrite.why\u0000İşlev fiili öbeğindeki: The noun in a light-verb phrase takes no article. Adding one single word makes the sentence look amateurish, and this distinction is tested at C1.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçedeki 'için' doğru: The English 'for' does not become 'für' here: sich bewerben takes the preposition 'um' (and 'bei' when you apply to a company).
task.rewrite.why\u0000Yazıldığı gibi „duvarda: As written it means „I am hanging it while it is already on the wall“. The picture moves towards the wall, so the preposition takes the accusative.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Yan cümle cümlenin ilk: The subordinate clause counts as the first element, so the finite verb comes straight after the comma and the subject moves behind it.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Her şey fantastik olunc: If everything is fantastic there is nothing left to say about what is genuinely good; once the top of the scale is used up, praise stops carrying information.
task.rewrite.why\u0000'zwar' cümlenin başında: If 'zwar' opens the sentence it is the first element; the finite verb follows straight after it (ist das Zimmer) and the subject slides into third place.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Almanca'da hasta birine: In German this is EXPECTED when somebody is ill; leaving it out reads as coldness. It is not an optional courtesy but a standard part of one.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Almanca eksikliği sorar: German asks about what is missing: „what are you LACKING?“ — the opposite of the English „what is the matter with you?“. The answer comes in the dative too: „Mir fehlt nichts.“
task.rewrite.why\u0000„Mal sehen“ Almanca'da: „Mal sehen“ is not rude in German but it counts as EMPTY — the other person is waiting for a new date. Naming a concrete day is the courtesy itself.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe '-dikten sonra': English already steps the tenses back ('after we had read'). German does the same: a nachdem clause has to sit one step behind the main clause — hatte/war + Partizip.
task.rewrite.why\u0000weil fiili sona atar; d: weil sends the verb to the end; denn does not. The two are close in meaning but not in word order — with denn, 'denn ich muss arbeiten' would have been right.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe 'çalışmak istiyo: English 'I want to work' is just as blunt in a formal application as German 'ich will'. The Konjunktiv II (würde … gern) makes the request polite.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Böyle yazılınca anlam t: Written like that the meaning flips: 'the dress likes me'. With gefallen the thing liked is the subject and the person who likes it stands in the dative.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Almancada vurgu ilk kon: German marks emphasis by what comes first. A sentence that starts with its subject stays neutral; English does that job with intonation or a cleft, so the step is easy to miss.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Zaman zarfı geleceği za: The time adverb already shows the future, so everyday German uses the present, exactly as English says 'next week I start'; putting werden into every sentence formalises the language.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Dilbilgisi kurulabilir: The grammar works, but German does not say it that way: when you hurt yourself the pronoun goes into the dative and the definite article replaces the possessive.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Fiil için edatı für'dür: The verb takes für; an goes with the noun — Interesse AN Kunst. Two structures carry the same meaning but their prepositions differ and cannot be swapped.
task.rewrite.why\u0000weil yardımcı fiili de: weil sends the auxiliary to the end as well: geübt habe. If the main clause order is to be kept, the conjunction had to be denn — the two are close in meaning, not in order.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Sürprizi duyurmak sürpr: Announcing the surprise ends the surprise. The turning point has to show itself; the moment the narrator names it the listener starts waiting and the effect is gone.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Edilgen çatı Partizip I: The passive is built with Partizip II + werden, as in the English 'must be reported'. The bare infinitive (melden) is not enough; German wants the participle (gemeldet).
task.rewrite.why\u0000hören = duymak, sehen =: hören = to hear, sehen = to see. On the phone you do not SEE the other person. „Auf Wiedersehen“ is a face-to-face goodbye; saying it on the phone is the commonest learner slip.
task.rewrite.why\u0000dass yan cümlesinde çek: In a dass clause the finite verb goes right to the end. English keeps its ordinary order inside a that-clause, so the German order has to be built deliberately every single time.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Dolaylı soru bir yan cü: An indirect question is a subordinate clause, so the finite verb goes last: geht. English drops the question order as well, but German goes further and sends the verb all the way to the end.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe '-diğinde' tek s: English 'when' does not separate a single occasion from a repeated one either. German does: an event that happened ONCE in the past takes als; wenn describes what is repeated (jedes Mal, wenn …).
task.rewrite.why\u0000İsimleşmiş hâlde hata v: In the nominalised version there is a failure but nobody who failed. Putting the agent back shortens the sentence and makes the responsibility visible — at C1 the choice between the two is made deliberately.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Belirsizlik varsa çözüm: If there is uncertainty the answer is to move the date, not to suspend it. A date with a proviso is not a commitment; no default arises, and without default there is no claim either.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe '-mesi için' tek: English has both shapes as well, 'in order to' and 'so that', and German picks between them the same way: SAME subject → um … zu, DIFFERENT subject → damit. Here the subject moves from ich to meine Kinder, so damit.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Edilgen Perfekt'te yard: In the passive Perfekt the auxiliary is shortened: worden, not geworden. English has one 'has been' for both, so the distinction slips easily; German keeps two separate forms here.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Bildirme kipiyle yazınc: Written in the indicative, the paper takes the accusation on itself; naming a source is not enough. The Konjunktiv I ties the claim to whoever made it and keeps the reporter out of it legally as well.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Bildirme kipiyle aktarm: Reporting in the indicative makes the reporter a party to the truth of the matter. For an interpreter or a journalist that is a loss of neutrality; the Konjunktiv I builds the distance into the grammar.
task.rewrite.why\u0000trotz resmî dilde tamla: In formal usage trotz takes the genitive: des vollen Programms. The dative is heard in speech and is not counted as wrong, but in writing and in a presentation it gives your level away at once.
task.rewrite.why\u0000vermeintlich „öyle deni: vermeintlich means „supposedly, but in fact not“; the rest of the sentence does not fit that. For a guess that has something behind it you need wohl or vermutlich — this mix-up is expensive in a written record.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Otoriteye başvurmak den: An appeal to authority moves the checking to where nobody does it. A solid claim rests on a source the other side can test — its strength lies not in the name of the source but in its accessibility.
task.rewrite.why\u0000İndirim hakkı ayıbın va: The right to reduce the rent arises not from the defect but from the notice and the passing of the deadline. A tenant who skips the sequence can lose while being in the right — in legal language the order of the steps matters more than the content.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe ismi rahatça tek: English avoids the repetition too, with 'the latter' or a pronoun, and German factual prose is stricter still: the reader is assumed to remember. Writing the same phrase a third time is no grammar mistake, but it makes the text read like a translation.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede '-e rağmen' fi: English 'although' does not move the verb either. German obwohl opens a subordinate clause: the finite verb (bin) goes last. And because the clause comes first, the main clause starts with its verb too (arbeite ich).
task.rewrite.why\u0000Deyimdeki artikel dilbi: The article in an idiom is not a grammatical choice, it is part of the fixed phrase. „seinen“ looks logical but breaks the idiom, and the sentence sounds foreign to a native ear — that sensitivity is exactly what is tested at C1.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Yan cümle başta olduğun: When the subordinate clause comes first the main clause starts with the verb; and „trotzdem“ belongs to speech, while formal writing prefers „gleichwohl“. Two faults sit together here and both drop the register of the text.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Olumsuzlanan bir şeyin: If what is negated is being replaced by the right thing, the conjunction is sondern, not aber. English uses 'but' for both, so the distinction disappears easily and the sentence opens an argument instead of settling one.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Varsayım yapısının bütü: The whole value of the hypothesis lies in claiming nothing. Adding „also gebe ich Ihnen recht“ at the end cancels the structure, and the speaker has given up both their position and the tool.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede 'o kadar' cüml: English says 'the better I understand' — the comparative comes first there too, but the subject keeps its place. In German the comparative (besser) is followed by the finite verb (verstehe) and only then the subject; in the je half the verb goes last (lerne).
task.rewrite.why\u0000Etken Perfekt haben ile: The active Perfekt is built with haben, the passive Perfekt with sein. The object becomes the subject and the shortened worden replaces geworden. The agent (die Stadt) is unimportant here and is dropped — that is what the passive is for.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe sıfat-fiil edat: English leaves the preposition stranded at the end ('the house I live in'). German puts the preposition the verb wants (wohnen IN) IN FRONT of the relative pronoun, and that preposition decides the pronoun's case: in + Dativ → in dem.
task.rewrite.why\u0000İki cümle aynı olguyu b: The two sentences report the same fact, but the first also passes judgement on whoever made the decision. If those people are sitting in the meeting, the idiom shifts the discussion from the fact to the person — at C1 the choice of idiom is a question of strategy, not of politeness.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Yapı dilbilgisi olarak: The structure is grammatically flawless, but fourteen words sit between the article and the noun and the reader does not know what is being talked about until the end. Any modifier longer than four words is unpacked into a relative clause or into two separate sentences.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe 'ama' hem aber h: English 'but' covers both aber and sondern, so both look right. German separates them: if what follows CORRECTS a negative statement, sondern is obligatory. 'aber' does not correct the negative, it adds a reservation to it.
task.rewrite.why\u0000İki yarının öznesi aynı: If both halves have the same subject, um … zu is preferred; damit is only needed when the subjects differ. English 'so that' does not make this distinction, so a speaker of English tends to build damit even with one subject - not wrong, but heavy.
task.rewrite.why\u0000bestehen auf yönelme hâ: bestehen auf takes the dative: auf einem neuen Gerät. English 'insist on' carries no case information, so the German preposition-and-case pair has to be learnt by heart; and since auf can take either case, guessing does not help.
task.rewrite.why\u0000'seit gestern' süren bi: 'seit gestern' points to a state that lasts, so sein is needed. With werden the sentence slides into 'the flat has been being made ready since yesterday'. English says both of them with 'is', so the distinction is easy to miss.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„scheinbar“ hastalığın: „scheinbar“ implies that the illness was faked, while the second half says he was excused — the sentence contradicts itself. English has the same pair (supposedly / apparently); the trap is that scheinbar looks like the word for what is apparent.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Kayıt değişimi tek keli: A change of register is not one word: wegen becomes aufgrund, the verb moves into the passive, and the everyday 'dicht machen' gives way to the term 'aussetzen'. Formal German names the process instead of the agent — the three changes travel together.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Deneyim anlatımında üç: Piling three adjectives on top of each other says nothing about an experience; the reader does not learn what was like what. Nominalising it -beim Auftritt, die Stimmung der Menge- names the event and the moment, so a single adjective becomes enough.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe 'tarafından' hâl: English 'by' asks for no case, so 'von' is taken for a label rather than a preposition and the noun is left as it stands. In German von ALWAYS takes the dative: von der Behörde, von dem Amt, von den Kollegen — the subject form (die Behörde) never appears here.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Ortaç sıfatı ilgi cümle: A participial attribute squeezes the relative clause between the article and the noun, and the time and place adverbs move in there too. English does this on a small scale ('the recently broadcast recordings'), but German fits whole phrases in and the participle takes an adjective ending.
task.rewrite.why\u0000İlgi cümlesi edilgen ol: The relative clause is passive, so Partizip II is needed; Partizip I would slide into 'the manual is updating something'. The rule: a passive or finished action takes Partizip II, an ongoing and active one takes Partizip I. The adverb -gerade- moves in front of the participle, after the article.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Konjunktiv II burada ki: Here the Konjunktiv II is not politeness but negotiating technique: the figure is said plainly, but the form makes stepping back less embarrassing. 'Ich will' leaves room for one answer only - yes or no. English does the same job with 'I was thinking of ten percent'.
task.rewrite.why\u0000dessen ve deren SAHİBİN: dessen and deren are chosen by the gender of the OWNER, not of the thing owned: die Autorin is feminine, so deren comes, whatever the gender of the Schicht behind it. And the noun in the relative clause takes no article — 'deren die Schicht' does not exist.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe mastar tek parça: English always puts 'to' in front of the verb, so 'zu' is either left out or thrown in front of it. In German, with a SEPARABLE verb, zu slips BETWEEN the prefix and the stem: zu-bereiten → zu-zu-bereiten. With an inseparable verb it stands normally: zu verstehen.
task.rewrite.why\u0000sollen öznel kip olarak: sollen used subjectively means 'other people say so' and replaces a long source phrase like 'nach Angaben von …' with a single word. English does the same job with 'is said to be'; the difference is that German loads it onto a modal verb.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Konjunktiv II burada ta: The Konjunktiv II does not weaken the request here, it opens it to negotiation: the other side can say 'not tomorrow, but the day after'. The date and the content stay exactly as they were; all that changes is that an answer becomes possible. English 'could you' does the same job.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Almanca adlaştırılmış b: German can turn a nominalised adverbial of manner -durch dreimaliges Wiegen- into an indem clause; the result reads better and says who did what. The English 'by -ing' form repeats no subject, whereas German makes the subject compulsory inside the clause.
task.rewrite.why\u0000obwohl ile trotz aynı k: obwohl and trotz build the same contrast but want different things: obwohl a subordinate clause, trotz a noun phrase in the genitive. English keeps them apart too, 'although' against 'despite', so the pairing is already familiar - what is new is the genitive.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Adlaştırma yalnız yer k: Nominalisation does not only save space, it also deletes the subject. Opening it back up forces you to choose one, and what the headline did not say appears exactly there. That is why turning nominalisations back into sentences as you read is the quickest reading exercise there is.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede 'en' TEK sözcü: English uses ONE word, 'best', for the adjective and the adverb alike ('the best roast' · 'it tastes best here'), so the two German forms get mixed up. German separates them: BEFORE A NOUN der/die/das beste (a declined adjective), MODIFYING A VERB am besten (an invariable adverb).
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede 'var' bir yükl: In English 'there is a big advantage' the noun is the subject, so the subject form is chosen in German too. In German 'es' is already the subject; what follows it is the OBJECT and takes the accusative: einen großen Vorteil, einen kleinen Nachteil.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede 'güvendiğim ar: English 'the friend I trust' shows no case either, so the pronoun is taken for an object and the accusative (den) is chosen. In German the VERB decides the case: vertrauen, helfen, begegnen, verzeihen and gefallen take the dative → dem. It is the verb's demand, not the meaning, that has to be learnt.
task.rewrite.why\u0000belegen kanıt yükü en y: belegen carries the heaviest burden of proof and a survey of forty people does not carry it. Learners often go too far here, because cautious verbs can sound like weakness — in German academic writing it is the other way round, and an unmeasured claim lowers your credibility.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe 'bu yüzden' cüml: English 'so' and 'that is why' do not disturb the word order, so the subject is left where it is. In German deshalb is NOT A CONJUNCTION BUT AN ADVERB: it is the first element, the finite verb comes straight after it, and the subject slides into third place. The same rule holds for trotzdem and deswegen.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe 'sigarayı bırakt: English 'I gave up smoking' takes a direct object, so an accusative object is put in German too. German gives 'aufhören' no direct object: it links either with mit + Dativ (mit dem Rauchen aufhören) or takes an infinitive with zu (aufhören zu rauchen).
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe araç bildirmeyi: English says 'by train' with a BARE NOUN and no article ever comes up, so the bare noun is written in German too. German wants mit + DATIVE and the article does not drop: mit dem Zug, mit der Bahn, mit dem Auto. The one exception is 'zu Fuß'.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede tek fiil var (: English already splits this: 'look forward to' for what is still to come, 'be pleased about' for what has happened. German loads the same split onto the preposition: sich freuen AUF for what has NOT HAPPENED yet, sich freuen ÜBER for what HAS. Both take the accusative; only the time differs.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„Du musst einfach“ zorl: „Du musst einfach“ makes light of the difficulty and „das ist keine große Sache“ invalidates what the other person went through. Advice that works gives a concrete step and says honestly how long it took — only then does the comparison encourage; otherwise it opens a distance.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe karşılaştırmayı: English already splits it: 'harder than' against 'as hard as'. German does the same: NOT EQUAL takes als (schwerer als, mehr als), EQUAL takes so … wie (so schwer wie). Wherever there is a comparative (-er), als follows.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„Du hast recht, aber …“: „Du hast recht, aber …“ gives everything away first and takes it back afterwards, and it stays unclear what was actually granted. German argument advances by distinguishing rather than by contradicting: „insofern …, als …“ limits exactly what is conceded and shows where the objection lands.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede zarflar öznede: English tends to put them the other way round — manner, place, then time. In German the middle of the sentence is almost fixed: TIME → MANNER → PLACE (wann, wie, wo). Fronting the place does not make the sentence wrong, but it always sounds foreign.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede beğenen kişi Ö: In English the person who likes is the SUBJECT ('I like the film'), so 'ich' is made the subject in German too. German turns it round: the thing liked is the subject and the person moves into the dative. The same pattern holds for fehlen, schmecken, passen and gehören — the verb agrees with the subject, not with the person.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede yan cümle önde: In English the main clause keeps its order even when the subordinate clause comes first ('when we arrived, the camp was full'), so the subject is left where it is. In German the whole subordinate clause is the FIRST ELEMENT and second place belongs to the verb. That is why the verb comes straight after the comma and the subject after it.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede ilgi zamiri yo: English has a relative pronoun but hardly marks its case, so there is little to lean on and the case of the main clause gets carried across. The pronoun's case comes from its job in the SUBORDINATE clause: here 'er hat mir geholfen' — the subject of that clause, so the nominative: der.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede dönüşlülük fii: English has no reflexive here at all — you simply hurry — so the pronoun drops out completely. With German verbs like sich beeilen, sich freuen, sich befinden and sich verhalten the pronoun is PART of the verb and changes with the subject: ich mich, du dich, er sich.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede sıfat HİÇ çeki: English adjectives NEVER inflect and do not change with their position ('a small box' · 'the box is small'), so two mistakes appear at once: the adjective in front of the noun gets no ending (klein → kleine) and the one in the predicate gets an extra one (alte → alt). German declines only in front of a noun.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Almanca övgüde ağırlığı: In German praise the weight comes from detail rather than from height: naming a particular part shows that somebody really listened. Very warm praise is often read the wrong way — as ingratiating, or as the run-up to a request; the person receiving it is embarrassed and does not know what to say.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede dönüşlülük fii: English has no case on a reflexive at all, so one form (mich) gets used for everything. German separates them: if there is ANOTHER object in the sentence the reflexive moves into the dative — ich wasche mich, but ich wasche mir die Hände; ich überlege mir das, ich wünsche mir etwas.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede '-ip -mediğini: English uses 'if' for both, so both of them become wenn. German separates them: an indirect YES/NO question takes ob ('whether I will manage it'), a real condition takes wenn ('if I manage it'). If 'or not' can be added after it, ob is the one.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede 'koymak' ve 'd: English has two verbs as well, 'put' and 'stand', but no case to choose ('on the table' either way). German wants both at once: MOVEMENT takes stellen/legen/setzen + accusative, POSITION takes stehen/liegen/sitzen + dative. The two decisions are made together.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede iki nesnenin s: English reorders them too ('I gave him the book' but 'I gave it to him'), though it adds a 'to'. In German the rule depends on whether the object is a PRONOUN: with two nouns the dative comes first (ihm das Buch), but an accusative PRONOUN moves in front (es ihm).
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede '-dığı için' v: English already separates them: 'because' takes a clause, 'because of' takes a noun. German does the same and adds a case: weil links a CLAUSE (the verb goes last), wegen takes a NOUN and wants the genitive — wegen der Krankheit, wegen des Wetters.
task.rewrite.why\u0000weder … noch yapısının: The weder … noch structure is negative in itself and no second nicht goes inside it. English 'neither … nor' works the same way, so the trap is a smaller one here — but it opens as soon as the sentence grows long and the negation is repeated out of habit.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Referans mektubu kişiyi: A reference puts the work before the person: a participial attribute ties the contribution to the noun, and the passive pushes whoever decided into the background. The result carries the same information but reads as a recorded fact rather than a personal opinion - which is exactly what such texts are after.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede 'gelmek istiyo: English puts 'to' in front of both ('want to come', 'hope to come'), so zu gets put in front of every infinitive. In German the MODAL verbs (wollen, können, müssen, dürfen, sollen, möchten) and lassen take a BARE infinitive; zu comes only with the other verbs (hoffen, vorhaben, versuchen, anfangen).
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe 'onaylandı' hem: English 'was approved' covers the event and the state alike, so the distinction is invisible. German separates them: WURDE genehmigt is an EVENT (the approving happened last week), WAR genehmigt is a STATE (it was already approved at that point). 'letzte Woche' gives a point in time, so an event is what is meant.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe '-mek yerine' te: English says 'instead of driving' with an -ing form and no subject, but learners take 'statt' for a conjunction and put a full clause after it. German wants an INFINITIVE with zu here: statt zu fahren, statt zu schätzen, statt Angst zu haben. The subject is named only in the main clause.
task.rewrite.why\u0000je-desto iki niceliği b: je-desto ties two quantities together and wants a comparative in both halves. English 'the more … the faster' builds the same relation, but the order matters: in German the first half is a subordinate clause and its verb goes last; in the second half the verb comes straight after the desto phrase.
task.rewrite.why\u0000als ob Konjunktiv II is: als ob takes the Konjunktiv II, because the structure already describes something that is not the case: it sounded that way but was not. English 'as if' does not change the verb, so a speaker of English tends to carry on in the indicative - 'als ob alles geklärt ist' sounds right and is not.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe karşılaştırmayı: English has irregular comparatives of its own (good → better → best), so the idea is familiar and only the list is different. In German a few very common words cannot be produced by rule: gern → lieber → am liebsten, viel → mehr → am meisten, gut → besser → am besten, hoch → höher → am höchsten.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede ilgi cümlesi t: English uses 'that' after 'everything' as well, so 'das' gets chosen by default. German looks at what comes before: after an INDEFINITE antecedent (alles, etwas, nichts, viel, das) the relative pronoun is WAS. After a definite noun it is der/die/das.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede 'veri' ve 'mas: English treats 'data' as a singular as often as not, so a singular article and a singular verb get chosen in German. In German these nouns are PLURAL ONLY: die Daten, die Kosten, die Leute, die Eltern, die Ferien. They have no singular — the article and the verb both have to be plural.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„Ich ordne an“ talimat: „Ich ordne an“ is the language of instruction and it presupposes authority; what follows, „vielleicht … eventuell“, is weaker than a suggestion. Mood and content cancel each other out: the speaker has both overstepped and said nothing. In a crisis you pick the level: vorschlagen, anordnen, in Kraft setzen.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Teselli cümlesi konuşan: A consoling sentence relieves the speaker rather than the listener; on top of that it makes a promise about the future that it cannot keep. A question in the Konjunktiv II invites the other person into their own situation - English does the same with 'how would you feel in her place', and the verb changes there too.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede 'çoğu' ve 'bir: English already makes these plural ('most employees are satisfied'), so the idea is familiar. German marks it in three places at once: the noun goes plural (Angestellten, Kollegen), the adjective takes -en, and the verb is plural as well (sind, sagen).
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede 'tatlı bir şey: English says 'something sweet' with a bare adjective, so a bare adjective is written in German too. German NOMINALISES it here: after etwas/nichts/viel/wenig the adjective is capitalised and takes -es — etwas Süßes, nichts Warmes, viel Interessantes.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede geçmiş tek ekt: English uses 'have' for every verb ('I have come', 'I have turned'), so there is no auxiliary to choose and haben gets used by default. German verbs of MOVEMENT and CHANGE OF STATE want sein: kommen, gehen, fahren, abbiegen, entstehen, werden. The rest are built with haben.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede çoğul TEK ekti: English has one plural ending and nothing after it, so a second ending is not expected. In German a plural noun takes -n in the DATIVE unless its plural already ends in -n: mit den Zuhörern, in den Hallen, von den Kindern. Plurals in -s are the exception (mit den Autos).
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede edat isme yapı: English keeps the preposition and adds a pronoun ('it depends on whether', 'I often think about it'), so nothing looks missing. German merges the preposition the verb wants with da-/dar- when it points at a clause or at something already said: davon abhängen, daran denken, darüber reden.
task.rewrite.why\u0000„wenn du das falsch ver: „wenn du das falsch verstanden hast“ puts the mistake on the receiver, „so war das nicht gemeint“ explains the intention without changing the effect, and the last part asks the person who was hurt to carry some of it as well. The German idiom hands the verdict to the receiver: angekommen. A short retraction with no justification is the only form that works.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede ettirgenlik bi: English has this too, with 'have' or 'get' ('have it examined'), so the idea is familiar and only the verb is different. Without 'lassen' the sentence means 'I will examine myself'. Having something done by somebody else is always built with lassen: schneiden lassen, reparieren lassen, geben lassen.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede sayıdan sonra: English already makes the noun plural after a number ('three onions'), so the idea is familiar. What is new is that the German plural cannot be guessed and is learnt with the word: Zwiebel → Zwiebeln, Frucht → Früchte, Karotte → Karotten.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe 'hareket ederek': English 'by moving a lot' has no subject and no finite verb, so a noun phrase is left standing in German. German builds the same meaning with a FULL subordinate clause: indem + subject + finite verb, the verb last. There is no subjectless indem clause — this is the structure that drops out most often, because the English -ing form has no German counterpart.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede gerçek dışı ko: English already builds two layers here ('if I had had more time, I would have come'), so the idea is familiar. But 'gehabt habe' is a REAL condition ('if I did have time'). An unreal past needs hätte/wäre + Partizip, in BOTH halves of the sentence.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede meslek adı cin: English job titles hardly ever change with gender ('architect' is the same for everybody), so the masculine form gets applied to everybody in German too. German builds the feminine with -in: Architekt → Architektin, Übersetzer → Übersetzerin, Ingenieur → Ingenieurin. The article changes with it (der → die) and the plural takes -innen.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe '%30 arttı' der: English separates them with 'by' and 'to': a rise of 30% is not a rise to that level. German does the same with two prepositions: um zehn Prozent = it went up by that much; auf zehn Prozent = it reached that level. The figure can stay the same while the two sentences say completely different things.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede 'çok' ve 'az': English already splits by countability — 'many trees' against 'much noise' — so the idea is familiar. German marks it with an ending instead: a COUNTABLE plural takes one (viele Bäume, wenige Läden), an UNCOUNTABLE noun does not (viel Lärm, wenig Zeit). The test is not the meaning but whether the noun has a plural.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede tamlama İKİ ay: English writes compounds as two words ('instruction manual', 'cash machine'), so they get written separately in German too. A German compound is ONE word, and splitting it is more than a spelling slip — the reader sees two independent nouns and the sense falls apart. Compounds with an abbreviation take a hyphen: EC-Karte, U-Bahn.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede malzeme ismin: English puts the material in front of the noun as a bare word ('a leather bag', 'a metal box'), so two nouns get written side by side in German. German picks one of two ways: either a COMPOUND (Ledertasche, Metallkasten) or aus + dative (eine Tasche aus Leder). Two separate words side by side is not one of them.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe 'bilmek' ikisini: English 'know' covers both, so the distinction is invisible and the two verbs get picked at random. German separates them: kennen for a PERSON, a PLACE or something familiar; wissen for a FACT, for information and for a clause. The short rule: kennen is followed by a noun, wissen by a subordinate clause.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede olumsuzluk fii: English puts the negation in front of the verb ('I did not pass the exam'), so it gets placed next to the verb in German too, right after the auxiliary. In German, if there is a definite object, nicht comes AFTER it. 'nicht die Prüfung' is right only when a contrast follows: nicht die Prüfung, sondern den Kurs.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede önek diye bir: English has prefixes but none that separate, so the participle gets built with a single pattern. German splits it in two: with a SEPARABLE verb (an-, ein-, auf-, mit-) the ge- slips BETWEEN the prefix and the stem — angeschlossen, eingeschaltet. With an INSEPARABLE verb (be-, ver-, ent-, unter-, über-) there is NO ge- at all — unterbrochen, verbunden, bezahlt.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Ünite 21 'statt … zu' k: Unit 21 practised the 'statt … zu' pattern; this is its sibling and it carries the same trap. English 'without getting angry' has no subject and no finite verb, so a noun or a bare adjective is left in German. After ohne, German wants an INFINITIVE with zu and names the subject only in the main clause: ohne zu fragen, ohne böse zu werden.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede süre ve ölçü y: English says 'for an hour' with a preposition, so 'für' or 'auf' gets added in German. German gives these WITHOUT a preposition, in the accusative: eine Stunde lang, zwei Meter hoch, drei Kilometer weit, den ganzen Tag. 'für' comes only with a PLANNED stretch of time (unit 20).
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe 'iki hafta sonra: English separates them with 'in' and 'after' ('in two weeks' against 'after two weeks there'), so the idea is familiar. German does the same: in zwei Wochen for a point counted from now, nach zwei Wochen for time that has passed since a beginning. The wrong choice pushes the sentence into the past or the future.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede '-den beri' il: English separates them with 'since' and 'for', but the German pair does not line up with it: a state that is STILL GOING takes seit + dative and the present tense ('seit drei Tagen krank'), while für describes a PLANNED stretch ('für eine Woche'). 'seit morgen' is impossible, because tomorrow has not started yet.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede mastar zaten i: English uses the -ing form as a noun and never changes the spelling ('getting up is hard'), so it gets left in lower case in German. When German nominalises an infinitive it writes it with a CAPITAL and gives it the neuter article: das Aufstehen, das Waschen, beim Anziehen, zum Lesen. Even when the article is hidden (beim = bei dem) the noun is there.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede beden bölümü İ: English uses a possessive with body parts ('I broke my finger'), so mein/meinen gets used in German — and the sentence is not ungrammatical, it simply does not sound German. The German pattern is this: the body part takes the DEFINITE article and whose it is comes in the dative — mir den Finger, mir das Knie, ihm die Hand.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede olumsuzluk tek: English already has both ('I have no idea' against 'that is not right'), so the idea is familiar; what is new is that German ties the choice to the noun. kein comes with an INDEFINITE or ARTICLE-LESS noun (keine Idee, kein Problem, keine Erfahrung); nicht negates a definite noun, a verb or an adjective.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede yüklem hiç hâl: English marks no case on a predicate either ('he is a good teacher'), but the rule 'verb → accusative' learnt earlier gets carried across. What follows sein, werden and bleiben is NOT AN OBJECT — it says the same thing as the subject and stands in the nominative: er ist ein guter Lehrer, sie wird Bürgerin, es bleibt ein Problem.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede 'sahile gitmek: English changes the preposition itself ('to the coast' against 'on the coast'), so when the German preposition stays the same the difference looks as if it has gone. In German the difference is IN THE CASE: direction takes the accusative (an die Küste fahren), place takes the dative (an der Küste wohnen). The same rule holds for an, auf, in, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben and zwischen.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede emir çıplak gö: The English imperative drops the subject as well ('take', 'wash'), so the pronoun gets left out in German too. A German formal imperative keeps the pronoun COMPULSORY: the verb first, 'Sie' straight after it in second place. Without the pronoun the sentence stops being an imperative and a subjectless fragment is left. Every imperative takes its own 'Sie' — it is repeated after the conjunction.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Öğrenci würde'yi tek ka: Learners take würde for a single pattern and attach it to every verb, because English 'would' does exactly that. German separates them: sein → wäre, haben → hätte, the modals → könnte/müsste/dürfte. These verbs carry their OWN Konjunktiv II and take no würde; würde is only the auxiliary for the rest.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede 'de/da' bir EK: English 'too' comes after the word it belongs to ('I clean the bathroom too'), so it gets put after the word in German as well. German auch and nur stand IN FRONT of what they emphasise — and the meaning changes with the position: 'Auch ich putze das Bad' (other people do it too) is not 'Ich putze auch das Bad' (I clean other rooms as well).
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede özne yoksa hiç: English already uses a dummy subject ('it is raining', 'it is getting colder'), so the idea is familiar. German does the same: weather, time and existential sentences take a placeholder with no meaning of its own — es regnet, es wird kälter, es gibt. 'es' cannot be translated, because it has no counterpart; but the sentence breaks without it.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede öznesiz cümle: English uses the dummy subject here as well ('it is necessary that you register'), so the idea is familiar. When German puts the clause at the end it sets a PLACEHOLDER at the front: es. Unit 22 dealt with the es of weather and existence; the job here is a different one — this es stands in for a whole CLAUSE, and it stays in place when that clause arrives.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe '-e/-a' üç yönü: English 'to' covers all three ('to Berlin', 'to Switzerland', 'to my sister'), so a single preposition gets chosen in German. German splits it three ways: nach for a city or a country with NO article (nach Berlin, nach Deutschland), in + accusative for a country WITH an article (in die Schweiz, in die Türkei), zu + dative for a PERSON or an institution (zu meiner Schwester, zum Arzt).
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede sıfat-fiil hiç: English participles never inflect ('an arrested person'), so a bare participle gets left in German. When German uses a Partizip II in front of a noun it declines it like an adjective, agreeing with whatever article is there: ein verhafteteR Mensch, die beschränktE Öffentlichkeit, das genannteN Beispiel. In the predicate it does not decline: der Mensch ist verhaftet.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Bu da bir özet: 45 ünit: This is a summary as well: one rule tested in three different places across 45 units. In a subordinate clause the finite verb goes RIGHT TO THE END (unit 3); if a modal stands beside it, the main verb comes first and the modal last (unit 19); a separable verb does NOT split in a subordinate clause but stays whole (zurechtkomme). And when the subordinate clause comes first, the main clause starts with its verb (unit 33).
task.rewrite.why\u0000nachdem yan cümlesi ana: A nachdem clause has to sit one tense-step behind the main clause: if the main clause is in the Perfekt, the subordinate clause goes into the Plusquamperfekt. English already carries this step ('after we had checked'), so the meaning is familiar; what gets left out in German is the form, because 'nachdem wir geprüft haben' sounds right and yet destroys the time relation.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Aracının işi cümlenin n: An interpreter's job is to convey what the sentence does — a literal translation carries a hope that is not there, while a correct one says that this is a polite refusal. But the second half goes further than that: a personal opinion and a generalisation get mixed into the translation. The moment it is noticed both sides withdraw their trust, and the person who was to be helped is left without an interpreter.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede 'satıcı olarak: English says 'as a saleswoman' with an article, so ein/eine gets added in German. After als in the sense of a job or a role German DROPS the article: als Verkäuferin arbeiten, als Ersatz dienen, als Treffpunkt nehmen. The same rule holds for bare job sentences: „Ich bin Verkäuferin.“
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede edilgen daima: The English passive always needs a subject as well, and 'I was burgled' is perfectly normal — but 'ich wurde eingebrochen' says the PERSON was broken open. German can build a passive with NO subject at all: neither an agent nor an object, and the sentence is still complete — bei mir wurde eingebrochen, hier wird gearbeitet, heute wird nicht geputzt.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede ismin kendisi: English nouns do not change for case at all, so the article gets changed and the noun is left as it is. Some German masculine nouns are WEAK: der Neffe, der Kollege, der Kunde, der Mensch, der Herr and der Student take -n or -en in every case but the nominative. der Onkel does NOT belong to this group and takes no ending.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe 'sıkılıyorum' de: English has exactly this pair — 'I am bored' against 'I am boring' — and German lines it up differently: 'ich bin langweilig' means 'I am boring'. The meaning flips and nobody corrects it, because the sentence is grammatically perfect. The right forms are mir ist langweilig or ich langweile mich. The same trap holds for interessiert (interested) against interessant (interesting).
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede 'buraya' ve 'o: English already marks this: you 'come here' and you 'go there', with the speaker as the point of reference. German splits it the same way but hangs it on the verb and the adverb: a direction AWAY from the speaker takes hin (dorthin, hingehen), a direction TOWARDS the speaker takes her (hierher, herkommen). A writer who is here says 'hierhergekommen', and going the other way, 'dorthin fahren'.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede yan cümlede de: English keeps its ordinary order in a subordinate clause ('because I have to get up early'), with the modal in front of the main verb. German turns that round: in a subordinate clause the MAIN verb comes first (aufstehen) and the modal goes RIGHT TO THE END (muss). The mistake comes from carrying the main clause order 'muss ich früh aufstehen' into the subordinate clause.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede ne bağlaç ne i: In English one word, 'that', is both the conjunction and the relative pronoun, so nothing keeps them apart to begin with. German separates them: dass is a CONJUNCTION and opens a subordinate clause (ich weiß, dass …); das is either an ARTICLE (das Projekt) or a RELATIVE PRONOUN (das Projekt, das beginnt). A quick test: if 'welches' can replace it, it is das; if not, dass.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede isimlerin cins: English nouns have NO gender at all, so the article is being guessed anyway, and with long compounds the guess gets worse. Yet the rule is exact and needs no learning by heart: the gender of a compound ALWAYS comes from the LAST part. der Schutz → der Umweltschutz, das Werk → das Kraftwerk, die Zone → die Fußgängerzone. The article of an unknown compound is not guessed, it is worked out.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede iyelik TEK ekt: English marks the possessive once, on the owner ('the contract's details'), so in German the article gets changed and the noun is left as it is. In German a masculine or neuter genitive is marked in TWO places: the article becomes des AND the noun itself takes -s or -es — des Vertrags, des Hauses, des Systems. In the feminine and the plural the noun does not change (der Firma, der Kosten).
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçe 'daha' ve 'bile: English has the pair already, 'only' against 'already', but the two get swapped because the German words resemble neither. The difference is a JUDGEMENT: erst = less than expected ('it is only seven, we still have time'), schon = more than expected ('the hall is already full'). The same figure, two different views — the rest of the sentence says which one is right.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede isim hiç değiş: English does have a few of these ('the accused', 'the unemployed') but they never change, so one form gets used in German too. Angestellte(r), Verwandte(r), Jugendliche(r) and Deutsche(r) come from adjectives and are declined LIKE ADJECTIVES: der Angestellte, ein Angestellter, die Angestellte, eine Angestellte. The weak masculines of unit 34 (der Neffe) were a different class — those always take -n, these change with the article.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Ünite 13 KİPLİ fiilleri: Unit 13 covered the MODAL verbs taking no zu. This is a separate class and the same rule holds: after gehen, kommen, lernen, helfen, sehen and hören the second verb is a BARE infinitive — ich gehe arbeiten, er lernt schwimmen, sie hilft mir tragen, ich höre ihn kommen. English puts 'to' in front of all of them ('learn to swim'), so a linking word gets inserted.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Türkçede geçmiş tek biç: English uses the simple past with modals as well ('I could not come', 'I had to work'), so the German rule is already familiar — the trap is that spoken German teaches the Perfekt first and the modals get pulled into it. German does not do that: können, müssen, dürfen, wollen and sollen take the Präteritum in the past (konnte, musste, durfte). The form 'habe gekonnt' appears only when the modal stands alone, and even then rarely.
task.rewrite.why\u0000Bu, 45 ünitede en çok t: This is the summary of the class of mistake that comes back most often across 45 units. English makes the person the subject in most of these ('I am cold', 'I do not like this route'), so 'ich' is made the subject in German too. In German the person moves into the DATIVE and something else is the subject: mir ist kalt, mir tut das Knie weh, mir gefällt der Weg. The same pattern holds for mir ist langweilig, mir macht es Spaß and mir wäre das nicht angenehm.

task.reply.prompt\u0000İlana kısa bir başvuru: Write a short application email about the advertisement. Say who you are, explain why you are applying in a sentence with a reason, and write when you could start.

task.reply.prompt\u0000Arkadaşının mesajına ö: Write an apologetic reply to your friend's message. Say with dass what you are sorry about, make clear it was not deliberate, and suggest something concrete to make up.
task.reply.prompt\u0000Bürgeramt'a bir randev: Write an email to the Bürgeramt asking for an appointment. Write what you are coming for, when you moved, which days suit you, and ask what you need to bring.

task.reply.prompt\u0000Aşağıdaki durumu bir e: Describe the situation below in a team report. Use at least three idioms — but keep the rule: idioms that describe the situation are allowed, idioms about a person are not. Do not accuse anybody, write the facts and your suggestion.
task.reply.prompt\u0000İnsan kaynaklarının ya: Write the sickness notification following the note from human resources. Give it a subject line, say what has happened and how many days you cannot come, state how you will send the certificate and write what will happen to the work.
task.reply.prompt\u0000Forumdaki soruya cevap: Write a reply to the question on the forum. Describe with wenn when you pick up your phone, estimate how long a day it takes, say what you would like to change and write whether that is doable for you.
task.reply.prompt\u0000Aşağıdaki metin deyiml: The text below is full of idioms. Rewrite it: keep at most TWO idioms (choose the ones that carry weight and do not stand out), throw the rest away and put at least two CONCRETE sentences in their place — a figure, a date or a detail. Do not lose any information.
task.reply.prompt\u0000Bu e-postaya cevap yaz: Write a reply to this email. Keep the order: recognise the feeling first, then set out the facts objectively, and present the solution last, as a question. Use a suggestion in the subjunctive at least once (Wäre es hilfreich, wenn …?) and build no accusation anywhere.
task.reply.prompt\u0000Arkadaşının mesajına c: Write a reply to your friend's message. Comfort them but do not CLOSE the subject: name exactly what the problem is, ask a question, and while you say what the good outcome could be, make clear you will be there for the bad one too. Avoid closing formulas of the „Das wird schon“ kind.
task.reply.prompt\u0000Aşağıdaki iki ifadeyi: Record the two statements below in a note for the minutes. The rules: report both statements in the Konjunktiv I, write your own observation in the indicative and separate it clearly, take nobody's side, and say at the end what can be verified and how.
task.reply.prompt\u0000Aşağıdaki iş örneğine: Give written feedback on the piece of work below. Keep to the German scale: do not inflate the praise, tie the shortcoming to the work rather than to the person, use at least one understatement („nicht schlecht“, „da ist noch Luft nach oben“, „sehr ordentlich“) and name a concrete next step.
task.reply.prompt\u0000Aşağıdaki sözleşme tas: Write a formal response to the draft contract below. Object to at most TWO clauses — pick the riskiest. In each objection: say in one sentence what the problem is, give the reason with its legal consequence, and propose a concrete alternative wording. The tone should propose a solution rather than make a demand.
task.reply.prompt\u0000Aşağıdaki yönetmelik c: Turn the regulation below into a notice that will go to the applicant. Apply the method: find the core first, list the conditions one under the other, turn the noun style into a verb style and name whoever does the acting. Lose no information; do not change the legal content, only make it readable.
task.reply.prompt\u0000Aşağıdaki çalışma için: Write an abstract for the study below (5-7 sentences). The rules: state the research question in one sentence, cover the method in one sentence, always write the RESULT, and choose the verb at the right level for each claim (nahelegen / aufzeigen / belegen). Make no claim the data does not carry; name a limitation yourself as well.
task.reply.prompt\u0000Aşağıdaki tebligata ka: Write an objection to the notice below that preserves the deadline. Let it have two parts: (1) a short and complete objection — against which decision, on whose behalf, stated plainly; (2) when the grounds will be submitted and why they are late. Do NOT write the grounds themselves — the job of this letter is to preserve the deadline. Keep the tone formal and short.
task.reply.prompt\u0000Aşağıdaki ret mektubu: The refusal letter below was written in four lines and found no response in its reader. Write a text that makes the same decision without using the reader up. Do not soften the decision — you are refusing; what changes is the register, not the information. Use at least one reference word (diesbezüglich / Letzteres / darauf) and one aside.
task.reply.prompt\u0000Aşağıdaki duruma dayan: Write a formal notice of defect to the landlord based on the situation below. Keep the order: describe the defect concretely and with its date, set a reasonable deadline for putting it right, state what happens if the deadline passes, and say that you will go on paying under reservation. Use no threatening language; write the consequence as a legal consequence.
task.reply.prompt\u0000Kriz toplantısının kar: Put the decisions of the crisis meeting into two texts. (A) A status notice for the team: level, authority, the interim fix and its limits, what will not be done today. (B) A notice for the customer: what is working, what is not, when the next update comes. The rule: GIVE NO FIX DATE, and call the interim fix an interim fix in both texts. Use the ready-made blocks.
task.reply.prompt\u0000Aşağıdaki olay notunda: Write TWO separate texts from the incident note below. (A) A short internal notice for the team channel — elliptical, technical, no apology. (B) A notice for the customers affected — full sentences, responsibility named, no technical detail, clear about what was done and what has changed so it does not happen again. Give the same facts in both; invent nothing and hide nothing either.
You are the one who made the joke. Write a short message to the person it affected. The rules: (1) do not defend your intention — „so war das nicht gemeint“ is banned; (2) do not explain why it was funny; (3) name concretely what was wrong (the target and the audience); (4) suggest one single next step. Do not grovel either — stay short and clear. Putting yourself down more than necessary also makes work for the other person.
task.reply.prompt\u0000Müzakere sonrası nihai: Send the final offer in writing after the negotiation. The rules: (1) list the three agreed points one by one and with their figures; (2) say that this is final and name the LIMIT OF YOUR AUTHORITY (so that it does not look like personal stubbornness); (3) use Konjunktiv II diplomacy in at least one place; (4) do not close the door — write in one calm sentence what happens if it is refused; (5) give a date. Use no threatening language.
